neutering-rabbits.summary: Rabbit neutering prevents uterine cancer and increases lifespan significantly. At Shivraj Pet Clinic we use specialised gas anaesthesia designed for small exotic animals.
neutering-rabbits.content:
Why Neutering Your Rabbit Matters

Uterine adenocarcinoma affects over 80% of unspayed female rabbits by age 5. It is the single most common cause of death in female rabbits.

🏥 At Shivraj Pet Clinic, we perform rabbit neutering using specialised exotic animal gas anaesthesia — one of very few clinics in PCMC qualified to do this safely.

Benefits of Neutering

  • Prevents uterine cancer — eliminates the #1 cause of death in females
  • Reduces territorial aggression — biting, lunging and spraying decrease significantly
  • Longer lifespan — 8–12 years vs 5–6 unneutered
  • Better bonding — calmer, more affectionate, easier to litter-train

The Procedure

  1. Pre-surgery blood test in our in-house lab
  2. Gas anaesthesia — gentle, monitored throughout
  3. Surgery: 20–35 minutes
  4. Recovery monitoring — closely watched
  5. Same-day discharge with written post-op care instructions
⚠️ Critical: Rabbits must NOT be fasted before surgery. Their digestive system must keep moving. This is a dangerous mistake made at non-exotic clinics.

Best Age to Neuter

Females: 4–6 months. Males: 3.5–5 months. Earlier is always better — cancer risk in females begins at 18 months.

how-to-know-rabbit-is-sick.title: How to Know If Your Rabbit Is Sick
how-to-know-rabbit-is-sick.summary: Rabbits, like most prey species, hide illness well. Learn the subtle signs that indicate your rabbit needs veterinary attention.
how-to-know-rabbit-is-sick.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

As a prey species, rabbits instinctively mask illness — which makes knowing the subtle signs more important than waiting for obvious ones.

Behavioral Signs

Reduced activity, hiding more than usual, reluctance to move, and reduced interest in food or interaction are early indicators.

Physical Signs

Changes in droppings, weight loss, a hunched posture, or a dull coat can all signal illness beneath the surface.

The Overall Rule

Any noticeable change from your rabbit's normal routine or behavior — even subtle — is worth a veterinary check rather than a wait-and-see approach.

Frequently Asked Questions

What's the fastest way to notice illness early?
Knowing your rabbit's normal daily habits closely enough to catch small deviations.

Are rabbits good at hiding pain?
Yes, extremely — this is an instinctive survival behavior.

Should any single odd behavior prompt a vet visit?
If it persists beyond a few hours or is combined with reduced appetite, yes.

dog-breathing-fast-resting.title: Dog Breathing Fast While Resting: Causes and Emergency Warning Signs
dog-breathing-fast-resting.summary: A dog breathing rapidly while resting — not after exercise — can signal pain, heart disease, or a respiratory emergency. Here's how to tell what's normal.
dog-breathing-fast-resting.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

Panting after a walk is normal. A dog breathing rapidly while lying still, relaxed, in a cool room, is not — and that distinction is the key to reading this symptom correctly.

What's Normal

A resting adult dog typically breathes at a slow, steady rate. Panting immediately after exercise, excitement, or in hot weather is expected and should settle within minutes once your dog cools down and calms down.

What's Not Normal

Rapid breathing at rest, with no obvious trigger, that persists for more than a few minutes is worth paying attention to — especially if it's paired with reluctance to lie down normally, blue-tinged gums or tongue, coughing, or visible effort with each breath.

Possible Causes

Heart disease, pain (including abdominal pain), fever, anemia, and primary respiratory or chest problems can all cause increased resting respiratory rate. The range of causes is wide enough that a home guess is unreliable — this is a symptom that benefits from an actual exam.

When It's an Emergency

Open-mouth breathing in a dog that doesn't normally pant, blue or pale gums, or breathing that looks labored (belly moving exaggeratedly with each breath) all mean immediate veterinary attention, not a wait-and-see period.

Frequently Asked Questions

How do I count my dog's resting respiratory rate?
Count chest rises for 30 seconds while your dog is calm and resting, then double it. Most healthy dogs fall in a normal range your vet can tell you for your dog's size — a rate that's climbing over time is more telling than a single count.

Can anxiety cause rapid breathing at rest?
Yes — situational stress can cause temporary rapid breathing, but it should settle once the trigger passes. Persistent rapid breathing with no clear trigger needs evaluation.

Is this more concerning in older dogs?
Yes — older dogs are more prone to heart and respiratory conditions that cause this symptom, so it should be taken seriously at any age but especially in seniors.

Should I take my dog's temperature at home?
If you have a proper pet thermometer, it can help, but don't delay a vet visit trying to gather more information first if breathing looks labored.

xray-detect-foreign-body-dog.summary: X-rays can catch many swallowed foreign objects in dogs, but not all. Here's what to know about detection limits.
xray-detect-foreign-body-dog.content:

"Did the X-ray find it?" is a common question after a dog swallows something — and the honest answer depends heavily on what was swallowed.

What X-Rays Detect Well

Dense objects like metal, bone, and stones are typically clearly visible on X-ray.

What Can Be Missed

Certain plastics, fabric, and some other materials may not show up clearly, even when present and causing obstruction.

What Happens If X-Ray Is Inconclusive

Additional diagnostics like ultrasound, or in some cases contrast studies, may be recommended if a foreign body is still suspected.

Yes, it's still a useful starting diagnostic step even without certainty about the object.

Can gas patterns alone suggest an obstruction?
Yes, abnormal gas patterns can be a helpful indirect sign even if the object itself isn't clearly visible.

What if the X-ray is clear but symptoms continue?
Further evaluation, including possible ultrasound, is typically recommended if symptoms persist.

rabbit-diarrhea-vs-cecotropes.title: Rabbit Diarrhea vs Normal Cecotropes: What Pet Parents Should Know
rabbit-diarrhea-vs-cecotropes.summary: Rabbits produce two types of droppings, and mistaking normal cecotropes for diarrhea is a common owner confusion. Here's the difference.
rabbit-diarrhea-vs-cecotropes.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

Rabbit droppings are more complex than they look — understanding the difference between normal cecotropes and true diarrhea prevents both unnecessary panic and missed emergencies.

What Are Cecotropes

These are soft, nutrient-rich droppings rabbits normally produce and re-ingest, usually not seen because rabbits eat them directly from the source.

What True Diarrhea Looks Like

Watery, loose stool that isn't the normal cecotrope pattern, especially combined with lethargy or reduced appetite, is a genuine concern.

When to Worry

Visible, uneaten soft droppings sticking to the rabbit, or true watery diarrhea, both warrant veterinary evaluation.

Frequently Asked Questions

Are cecotropes a sign of illness?
No, they're a completely normal part of rabbit digestion.

Why would cecotropes be visible instead of eaten?
This can indicate pain, obesity limiting reach, or dental issues preventing normal re-ingestion.

Is true diarrhea in rabbits an emergency?
Yes, it can indicate serious illness and dehydrates quickly.

dog-suddenly-weak-unable-stand.title: Why Is My Dog Suddenly Weak or Unable to Stand?
dog-suddenly-weak-unable-stand.summary: Sudden weakness or an inability to stand in dogs can stem from many causes — some minor, some critical. Here's how to assess it and when to act fast.
dog-suddenly-weak-unable-stand.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

A dog that suddenly can't get up is one of the more frightening things an owner can witness — and rightly so, because the list of possible causes ranges widely in urgency.

Possible Causes

Sudden weakness can stem from low blood sugar, anemia, internal bleeding, heart problems, neurological issues, spinal injury, poisoning, or severe pain. The wide range is exactly why this symptom needs a professional assessment rather than a guess.

What to Check Immediately

Look at gum color (pale or white gums suggest anemia or shock), check for obvious injury, and note whether your dog is alert and responsive or dazed. Don't force your dog to walk or stand if there's any suspicion of spinal injury.

Moving a Weak or Injured Dog Safely

If a spinal injury is possible, use a flat, firm surface as a makeshift stretcher rather than carrying your dog under the belly. Keep movement minimal and get to the clinic promptly.

Why This Is Always Treated as Urgent

Even when the cause turns out to be minor, sudden weakness or an inability to stand should be treated as an emergency until proven otherwise — the downside of waiting is far worse than the inconvenience of an unnecessary visit.

Frequently Asked Questions

Could this just be old age catching up?
Age-related joint or muscle weakness usually develops gradually, not suddenly — a sudden onset points toward an acute cause that needs evaluation.

My dog collapsed briefly then seemed fine — do I still need to go in?
Yes. A brief collapse can be caused by heart, neurological, or metabolic issues that won't necessarily show again immediately but still need investigating.

Can low blood sugar cause this in adult dogs, not just puppies?
Yes, though it's more common in puppies and small-breed dogs — certain medical conditions can cause it in adults too.

What tests help find the cause?
Bloodwork, a neurological exam, and sometimes imaging (X-ray or ultrasound) are typically used to narrow down the cause.

rabbit-vaccination-preventive-care-india.summary: Vaccination needs for pet rabbits in India differ from Western countries. Here's what preventive care actually looks like locally.
rabbit-vaccination-preventive-care-india.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

dog-seizures-what-to-do.title: Dog Seizures: What to Do During a Seizure and When to Seek Veterinary Care
dog-seizures-what-to-do.summary: Watching your dog have a seizure is frightening. Here's exactly what to do in the moment, and when a seizure means an emergency vet visit.
dog-seizures-what-to-do.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

A seizure in your dog looks alarming, but what you do in the first few minutes matters more than panic. Here's a clear, practical guide.

During the Seizure

Stay calm and keep your hands away from your dog's mouth — dogs don't swallow their tongues, and you risk being accidentally bitten. Clear the area of furniture or objects your dog could hit. Time the seizure if you can; duration is one of the most useful pieces of information for your vet.

After the Seizure

Dogs often experience a disoriented recovery period afterward — confusion, temporary blindness, or unsteady walking. Keep your dog in a quiet, dim space and avoid crowding them until they're fully oriented.

When It's an Emergency

A seizure lasting more than a few minutes, multiple seizures in a row without full recovery between them (cluster seizures), or a first-ever seizure in an adult or senior dog all require immediate veterinary attention.

Why the Cause Matters

Seizures can stem from epilepsy, toxin exposure, low blood sugar, liver disease, or brain conditions. A single seizure that resolves quickly still warrants a veterinary conversation, since identifying an underlying cause changes the management plan significantly.

Frequently Asked Questions

Should I put something in my dog's mouth during a seizure?
No — this is unnecessary and risks injury to both you and your dog.

How long is a seizure typically expected to last?
Most seizures last under two minutes; anything approaching or exceeding five minutes is an emergency.

Can seizures happen just once and never again?
Yes, but any first-time seizure should still be evaluated to rule out an underlying, treatable cause.

Is epilepsy the most common cause?
It's one of several possible causes and is generally considered after other causes like toxin exposure or metabolic issues are ruled out.

The Foundation: Hay

Unlimited, good-quality hay should make up the majority of a rabbit's diet — it drives dental wear and gut motility simultaneously.

Vegetables and Pellets

Fresh, rabbit-safe vegetables and a measured amount of quality pellets round out the diet, while sugary treats (including carrots in excess) should be limited.

What to Avoid

High-sugar treats, excessive pellets, and low-fiber diets are all linked to dental disease, obesity, and GI stasis.

Frequently Asked Questions

Are carrots bad for rabbits?
Not inherently, but they should be a small treat, not a dietary staple, due to sugar content.

How much hay does a rabbit need daily?
Roughly its own body size in hay volume, available at all times.

Can diet changes cause GI stasis?
Yes, sudden changes can disrupt gut motility — introduce changes gradually.

dog-eats-foreign-object.title: What to Do If Your Dog Eats a Foreign Object
dog-eats-foreign-object.summary: Your dog swallowed something they shouldn't have. Here's how to assess the risk, what to watch for, and when it's a surgical emergency.
dog-eats-foreign-object.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

Dogs, particularly young and curious ones, swallow objects that have no business being in a stomach — toys, socks, string, corn cobs, stones. What happens next depends heavily on the object and how quickly you act.

Why Some Objects Are More Dangerous Than Others

Smooth, small objects sometimes pass on their own. Sharp objects, string or thread (especially in cats but also dogs), and anything too large to pass through the intestines pose a much higher risk of obstruction or internal injury.

Call Immediately, Don't Wait for Symptoms

If you witnessed or strongly suspect ingestion, call your vet right away rather than waiting to see if symptoms develop. Depending on the object and timing, your vet may recommend inducing vomiting, monitoring, or imaging to locate it — this decision needs professional judgment, not a home guess.

Warning Signs of Obstruction

Repeated vomiting, refusal to eat, abdominal pain or a hunched posture, straining without producing stool, and lethargy together point toward a possible obstruction, which is a surgical emergency.

Diagnosis and Treatment

X-rays can identify many objects and abnormal gas patterns; some materials aren't visible on X-ray, in which case ultrasound or other diagnostics may be used. Treatment ranges from monitoring for natural passage to surgical removal, depending on the object and its location.

Frequently Asked Questions

My dog swallowed a small piece of a toy but seems fine — do I still need to call?
Yes — call and describe the object and size. Some things that seem fine initially cause problems days later.

Is string dangerous even if my dog isn't showing symptoms?
Yes, string can cause serious internal damage in some cases, particularly if one end lodges in place. Don't wait for symptoms — call your vet.

Can every foreign object be seen on an X-ray?
No — some materials, including certain plastics and fabrics, aren't visible on X-ray, and ultrasound or other methods may be needed.

How can I prevent this from happening again?
Supervise play with small or destructible toys, keep laundry and small household objects out of reach, and choose size-appropriate, durable toys.

dog-heatstroke-symptoms-first-aid.title: Dog Heatstroke: Symptoms, First Aid, and Emergency Treatment
dog-heatstroke-symptoms-first-aid.summary: Heatstroke in dogs escalates fast and can be fatal within minutes. Learn the early warning signs, immediate first aid steps, and when to rush to a vet.
dog-heatstroke-symptoms-first-aid.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

Indian summers make heatstroke a real, common, and dangerous risk for dogs — particularly flat-faced breeds, seniors, and dogs left in parked cars or without shade. Minutes matter here more than in almost any other emergency.

Early Warning Signs

Heavy panting that doesn't settle, bright red gums, excessive drooling, weakness, and disorientation are early signs. As it progresses, vomiting, collapse, and seizures can follow.

Immediate First Aid

Move your dog to a cool, shaded area immediately. Apply cool (not ice-cold) water to the body, particularly the belly, paws, and neck, and use a fan if available. Offer small amounts of cool water to drink if your dog is alert enough to drink safely. Do not use ice-cold water or ice directly on the skin — this can constrict blood vessels and actually slow cooling.

Get to a Vet Immediately, Even If Cooling Seems to Help

Heatstroke causes internal damage that isn't visible from the outside — even a dog that seems to recover with initial cooling needs veterinary evaluation for organ function, clotting, and hydration status.

Prevention

Never leave a dog in a parked car, even briefly, even with windows cracked. Walk during cooler hours, provide constant access to shade and water, and watch flat-faced breeds (Pugs, Bulldogs) and senior dogs especially closely, since they overheat faster.

Frequently Asked Questions

How quickly can heatstroke become dangerous?
Very quickly — it can escalate from early signs to a life-threatening state within minutes to an hour, which is why immediate action matters more than in most conditions.

Is it safe to use ice on my dog to cool them faster?
No — ice or ice-cold water can be counterproductive by constricting blood vessels near the skin. Use cool, not ice-cold, water instead.

Which breeds are most at risk?
Flat-faced (brachycephalic) breeds like Pugs and Bulldogs, along with senior dogs, overweight dogs, and thick-coated breeds, are all at elevated risk.

My dog seems fine after I cooled them down — do I still need a vet visit?
Yes — internal effects of heatstroke aren't visible externally and need to be checked.

Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

Parrots don't just get “sick” in one generic way — different diseases in companion birds have distinct causes, distinct warning signs, and distinct treatment paths. If you've already read our guide on Sick Bird Syndrome and know your parrot is hiding something, this is the next step: understanding what conditions are actually on the table, so you know what your vet is checking for and why. At Shivraj Pet Clinic & Lab, exotic bird cases are worked up individually — a cockatiel with feather loss and a macaw with breathing trouble are not the same diagnostic problem, even though both are “a sick bird.”

Respiratory Disease

Birds have a highly specialized respiratory system of lungs and air sacs, which means even a mild infection can escalate quickly. Watch for open-mouth breathing, tail bobbing while breathing, wheezing, nasal discharge, or a change in voice. Open-mouth breathing or an inability to perch normally is an emergency, not a wait-and-watch symptom.

Nutritional Deficiencies

An all-seed diet is one of the most common root causes of chronic illness in pet parrots. Sunflower seeds, millet, and peanuts are palatable but nutritionally incomplete — particularly for Vitamin A. Deficiency shows up as poor feather quality, higher infection susceptibility, and changes around the beak and skin. The fix isn't a supplement alone; it's a species-appropriate, formulated diet with fresh vegetables.

Feather Plucking

Plucking is frustrating for owners because it looks purely behavioral — but it isn't always. Stress, boredom, and hormonal changes can cause it, but so can skin irritation, parasites, pain, and underlying disease. Treating it as “just a habit” without a veterinary workup risks missing a medical cause entirely.

Digestive and Liver Problems

Reduced appetite, regurgitation, and changes in droppings are early digestive warning signs. Liver disease is a step further and more dangerous because it often produces very few visible symptoms until it's advanced — birds on high-fat, high-seed diets are at higher risk. Diagnostic testing, not observation alone, is what catches this early.

💡 Egg binding is a female-only emergency — a hen unable to pass an egg. Signs include straining, sitting at the bottom of the cage, swollen abdomen, and weakness. Small birds like budgies and cockatiels can deteriorate within hours. It does not resolve on its own and needs same-day veterinary attention.

Heavy Metal Toxicity

Curious birds chew on what's around them — old paint, metal toys, batteries, jewelry. Lead and zinc toxicity can cause weakness, digestive upset, seizures, and neurological signs. Diagnosis usually needs X-rays and lab testing, since the symptoms alone overlap with several other conditions.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can one parrot show signs of more than one condition at once?
Yes, and it's common — a bird on a poor diet is more prone to infection, feather problems, and liver strain simultaneously. That's why a full workup, not a single symptom check, matters.

Is feather plucking ever purely behavioral?
It can be, but only after medical causes — skin disease, parasites, pain, nutritional deficiency — have been ruled out first.

How is egg binding treated?
Treatment depends on the bird's condition and may include supportive care, calcium therapy, or manual assistance under veterinary supervision. Never attempt to manipulate an egg-bound bird at home.

Can heavy metal toxicity be prevented?
Largely yes — keep painted or metal objects, batteries, and jewelry out of reach, and supervise out-of-cage time.

dog-bite-wounds-veterinary-exam.summary: A small puncture from a dog bite can hide serious damage underneath. Here's why bite wounds need veterinary evaluation even when they look minor.
dog-bite-wounds-veterinary-exam.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

A dog bite wound often looks far less serious on the surface than it actually is — the visible puncture is frequently the smallest part of the injury.

Why Bite Wounds Deceive

Dog teeth cause crushing and tearing injury beneath the skin that a small surface puncture doesn't reveal. Damage to underlying muscle, or infection introduced deep into tissue, can be present even when the visible wound looks minor.

Infection Risk

A dog's mouth carries bacteria that can cause serious infection if introduced under the skin. Wounds that aren't properly cleaned and, when necessary, treated with antibiotics can develop abscesses or spreading infection days later.

What to Do Immediately

Gently clean the wound if you can do so safely, control any active bleeding with light pressure, and get to a vet promptly rather than assuming a small wound will heal on its own.

What Your Vet Will Check

Beyond cleaning and treating the visible wound, your vet will assess for deeper tissue damage, may recommend antibiotics to prevent infection, and will advise on wound monitoring over the following days.

Frequently Asked Questions

The wound looks tiny — do I really need to bring my dog in?
Yes — the surface size of a bite wound often has little relation to the damage underneath.

How soon after a bite can infection develop?
Infection can develop within a day or two, sometimes presenting as swelling, warmth, or discharge at the site.

Should I bandage the wound myself first?
Light, clean pressure to control bleeding is fine, but let your vet assess and properly clean and dress the wound rather than sealing it yourself.

Does this apply to bites from other animals too?
Yes — cat bites in particular carry a high infection risk due to their narrow, deep puncture wounds, and should also be evaluated promptly.

dog-ate-chocolate-first-hour.title: Dog Ate Chocolate? What to Do in the First Hour
dog-ate-chocolate-first-hour.summary: Your dog ate chocolate. Here's exactly what to check, what to do in the first 60 minutes, and when it's an emergency versus a false alarm.
dog-ate-chocolate-first-hour.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

The first hour after your dog eats chocolate is the window that matters most. Chocolate contains theobromine and caffeine, both of which dogs metabolize far more slowly than humans — and the danger depends heavily on the type of chocolate, the amount, and your dog's size. This is a step-by-step guide for that first hour, not a general toxic-foods list.

Step 1: Identify What and How Much

Check the wrapper. Dark chocolate, baking chocolate, and cocoa powder are far more dangerous than milk chocolate; white chocolate carries minimal risk. Estimate the amount eaten and your dog's weight — this is the single most useful piece of information you can give your vet on the phone.

Step 2: Call Before You Act

Do not induce vomiting at home without veterinary guidance — timing matters, and doing it incorrectly can cause more harm (aspiration, esophageal irritation) than benefit. Call your vet immediately with the chocolate type, quantity, and your dog's weight; they'll tell you whether this needs an in-clinic visit right now.

Step 3: Watch for Early Signs

Symptoms can take a few hours to appear and include restlessness, vomiting, diarrhea, increased thirst, a racing heart rate, and — in severe cases — tremors or seizures. Don't wait for symptoms to appear before calling; by the time signs show, absorption is already underway.

💡 Depending on timing and dose, treatment may include inducing vomiting under clinical supervision, activated charcoal to limit absorption, and monitoring heart rate and hydration. If your vet recommends an in-person visit, don't delay for a “let's see how he does” period.

What NOT to Do

Don't give salt, hydrogen peroxide without vet guidance on dosing, or human anti-nausea medication. Don't assume “he seems fine” means he's in the clear — toxicity can take hours to become visible.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much chocolate is actually dangerous?
It depends on chocolate type and your dog's weight — dark and baking chocolate are dangerous in much smaller amounts than milk chocolate. There's no safe universal threshold; always call your vet with the specifics.

My dog ate chocolate an hour ago and seems normal — are we in the clear?
Not necessarily. Symptoms can be delayed. A normal-looking dog an hour in doesn't rule out toxicity — call anyway.

Is white chocolate a concern?
Minimal theobromine content means low risk, but large quantities can still cause an upset stomach from the fat and sugar content.

What information should I have ready when I call?
Type of chocolate, estimated quantity, your dog's weight, and how long ago it happened.

sudden-paralysis-dogs.title: Sudden Paralysis in Dogs: Possible Causes and Why Immediate Care Matters
sudden-paralysis-dogs.summary: Sudden paralysis or loss of coordination in a dog's legs is a medical emergency. Learn the possible causes and why every hour of delay matters.
sudden-paralysis-dogs.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

Sudden paralysis — a dog that can't move its hind legs, or suddenly drags a limb — is one of the clearest signals that something serious is happening internally, and time to treatment directly affects the outcome in several of the underlying conditions.

Common Causes

Intervertebral disc disease (a slipped or herniated disc pressing on the spinal cord) is one of the most common causes, particularly in long-backed breeds like Dachshunds. Other causes include spinal trauma, fibrocartilaginous embolism, tick-borne diseases, and, less commonly, tumors affecting the spine or nerves.

Why Speed of Treatment Matters

For several spinal conditions, the amount of time the spinal cord is compressed or without blood flow directly affects how much function can be recovered. This is a condition where "let's wait and see if it improves" can cost your dog mobility that could otherwise have been saved.

What to Do

Keep your dog as still as possible during transport to avoid further spinal injury, and get to a vet immediately. Do not attempt to force your dog to walk or stand.

Diagnosis and Treatment

Diagnosis often involves a neurological exam and imaging — X-rays can rule out some causes, while advanced imaging (arranged through referral when needed) may be required for a full picture of spinal cord involvement. Treatment ranges from strict rest and medication to surgery, depending on severity and cause.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is this always a spinal problem?
Not always, but spinal causes are among the most common and time-sensitive, which is why immediate evaluation is important regardless of the suspected cause.

Which breeds are more prone to disc-related paralysis?
Long-backed breeds like Dachshunds, along with Beagles and Cocker Spaniels, are at higher risk of intervertebral disc disease.

Can partial paralysis improve on its own?
Some mild cases improve with strict rest and medical management, but this should be a veterinary-directed decision, not a home judgment call — the risk of waiting too long is significant.

What does the recovery process typically involve?
Depending on the cause and severity, this can range from weeks of restricted activity to physical rehabilitation or surgical intervention.

dog-urine-problems-uti-stones.title: Dog Urine Problems: Signs of UTI, Stones, and Urinary Blockage
dog-urine-problems-uti-stones.summary: Straining to urinate, blood in urine, or frequent accidents can signal a UTI, bladder stones, or a life-threatening blockage in dogs. Here's how to tell them apart.
dog-urine-problems-uti-stones.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

Urinary symptoms in dogs span a wide range of urgency — from a manageable infection to a blockage that can become fatal within a day. Here's how to read the signs.

Signs of a Urinary Tract Infection

Frequent urination in small amounts, straining, blood-tinged urine, and accidents in a previously house-trained dog are common UTI signs. Uncomfortable but generally not immediately life-threatening, a UTI still needs treatment to prevent it from ascending to the kidneys.

Bladder Stones

Stones can cause similar straining and blood in urine, sometimes progressing to a partial or complete blockage. Some stones are visible on X-ray, while others require ultrasound for detection.

Urinary Blockage — a True Emergency

A dog straining repeatedly and producing little or no urine, especially a male dog, may have a urinary obstruction. This is a life-threatening emergency — a blocked bladder can lead to kidney damage and dangerous toxin buildup within hours.

When to Go In Immediately

Straining with no urine output, visible distress, a swollen abdomen, or vomiting alongside urinary straining all mean immediate veterinary attention, not a next-day appointment.

Frequently Asked Questions

How do I tell a UTI apart from a blockage at home?
You often can't reliably — both cause straining. The key differentiator is whether urine is actually being produced. If not, treat it as an emergency.

Are male dogs at higher blockage risk than females?
Yes, due to a narrower urethra, though blockage can occur in females too.

Can diet affect stone formation?
Yes — certain diets can influence the risk and type of stones formed; your vet can recommend a preventive diet after diagnosis.

How is a blockage treated?
Treatment typically involves relieving the obstruction (often via catheterization) and addressing any resulting metabolic complications — this requires immediate, in-clinic care.

household-poisons-pets.title: Rat Poison, Plants & Household Chemicals: Hidden Poisons in Your Home
household-poisons-pets.summary: Beyond food — the household poisons pet owners overlook: rodenticide, common houseplants, and cleaning chemicals. What's dangerous, what to watch for, and what to do.
household-poisons-pets.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

Most poisoning conversations focus on food — chocolate, onions, grapes. But some of the most dangerous exposures in Indian homes have nothing to do with the kitchen: rat poison left out for pest control, ordinary houseplants, and cleaning products under the sink. These are the poisons that catch pet parents off guard because they don't look like “pet hazards” at all.

💡 Rodenticide (rat poison) is one of the most serious accidental poisonings in dogs and cats. Some formulations interfere with blood clotting — causing internal bleeding days later — which is exactly why it's dangerous even when your pet looks fine at first. If you know or suspect exposure, treat it as an emergency regardless of appearance.

Rodenticide (Rat Poison)

Common in homes and building common areas, different formulations cause different problems — some interfere with blood clotting, others cause severe neurological signs. Watch for lethargy, pale gums, unexplained bruising, difficulty breathing, or bleeding from the nose or gums, sometimes days after exposure.

Toxic Houseplants

Several common ornamental plants are toxic to dogs and cats, including lilies (especially dangerous to cats — even pollen contact can cause kidney failure), sago palm, oleander, and philodendron. Signs range from drooling and vomiting to, in severe cases, organ failure. If you're not sure whether a plant in your home is pet-safe, treat it as unsafe until confirmed otherwise.

Household Chemicals

Cleaning agents, disinfectants, drain cleaners, and pesticides stored within reach are a common cause of accidental exposure — usually through direct ingestion or licking a contaminated paw after walking through a freshly cleaned floor. Symptoms depend on the chemical but often include drooling, vomiting, mouth irritation, or breathing difficulty.

What to Do If You Suspect Exposure

Move your pet away from the source immediately. If you know what was ingested, keep the packaging — it tells your vet exactly what they're dealing with. Do not induce vomiting unless a vet tells you to; some chemicals cause more damage coming back up than staying down. Call your vet right away, even before symptoms appear.

Frequently Asked Questions

My pet walked near rat poison but I didn't see them eat it — should I still worry?
Yes. If exposure is possible, call your vet. The delayed-bleeding types of rodenticide are dangerous precisely because early signs are easy to miss.

Are all lilies dangerous, or just some varieties?
Most true lilies are considered highly toxic to cats specifically. If you have cats, it's safest to avoid lilies in the home entirely.

My dog just licked a freshly mopped floor — is that a problem?
Depends on the cleaning agent. Keep pets off freshly cleaned floors until fully dry, and check the product label for pet-safety information.

Should I keep poison control information on hand?
Yes — save your vet's emergency number where you can find it quickly. In a real exposure, minutes matter.

dog-drinking-too-much-water.title: Why Is My Dog Drinking Too Much Water?
dog-drinking-too-much-water.summary: Increased thirst in dogs can be an early sign of diabetes, kidney disease, or other conditions. Learn when excessive drinking warrants a vet visit.
dog-drinking-too-much-water.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

It's easy to dismiss a thirstier-than-usual dog as "just the weather" — but a genuine, sustained increase in water intake is one of the more reliable early indicators that something metabolic is going on internally.

What Counts as Excessive

Normal water intake varies by dog, but a noticeable, sustained increase — refilling the bowl far more often, drinking immediately after finishing, or accidents from a previously house-trained dog — is worth tracking rather than dismissing.

Possible Causes

Diabetes, kidney disease, Cushing's disease, liver disease, and certain infections can all cause increased thirst and urination as an early sign, often before other symptoms become obvious.

Why Early Detection Matters Here

Several of these conditions are more manageable when caught early, before complications develop. Increased thirst is frequently one of the first visible clues, which makes it worth acting on rather than waiting for more symptoms to appear.

What Diagnosis Involves

Bloodwork and urine testing are typically the starting point, since blood glucose, kidney values, and urine concentration can point toward the underlying cause fairly directly.

Frequently Asked Questions

Could hot weather alone explain this?
It can explain a moderate increase, but a dramatic or sustained change — especially alongside more frequent urination — deserves veterinary evaluation rather than assuming it's just the heat.

Is this more concerning in senior dogs?
Yes — several of the underlying conditions are more common in older dogs, making evaluation especially worthwhile in seniors showing this symptom.

Does increased thirst always mean disease?
Not necessarily, but a genuine, sustained change is worth investigating rather than assuming it's benign.

What tests are usually done first?
Bloodwork and a urine test are the standard starting point for identifying the cause.

acral-lick-dermatitis-dogs.title: Acral Lick Dermatitis in Dogs — Why Your Dog Won't Stop Licking One Spot
acral-lick-dermatitis-dogs.summary: Constant paw or leg licking can turn into a painful, thickened wound called a lick granuloma. Learn the causes, treatment, and prevention of acral lick dermatitis from Shivraj Pet Clinic, Pune.
acral-lick-dermatitis-dogs.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine) — 24+ years of experience in companion animal and exotic pet medicine.

If your dog keeps returning to the same spot on a paw or leg to lick, chew, or gnaw — sometimes for hours a day — you may be watching the early stages of acral lick dermatitis, also called a lick granuloma. At Shivraj Pet Clinic, Wakad & Pimple Saudagar, Pune, this is one of the more frustrating conditions we treat, because the licking itself becomes part of the problem, not just a symptom of it.

Quick Facts

Species affectedDogs (most commonly large, active breeds)
SeverityMild to severe — chronic cases cause deep tissue infection
Common causesAllergies, anxiety/boredom, joint pain, parasites, skin infection
Emergency signsOpen bleeding wound, foul odour, visible bone or tendon
PreventionExercise, mental stimulation, parasite control, early allergy management

What Is Acral Lick Dermatitis?

Acral lick dermatitis develops when a dog repeatedly licks one localised area — almost always the front paw or lower leg — until the constant moisture and trauma cause inflammation, hair loss, and a thickened, raised patch of skin called a granuloma. What starts as a habit becomes self-perpetuating: the licking itself irritates the skin further, which triggers more licking.

Common Causes

  • Allergies — environmental or food allergies causing localised itching
  • Anxiety or boredom — a compulsive behaviour similar to nail-biting in humans, often seen in dogs left alone for long hours
  • Underlying pain — arthritis or an old joint injury can cause a dog to lick the area over the joint
  • Parasites — fleas or mites causing localised irritation
  • Skin or deep tissue infection — bacterial infection can both cause and result from chronic licking
🔍 Clinical insight: At Shivraj Pet Clinic, we frequently see lick granulomas in dogs that appear otherwise perfectly healthy — the underlying trigger is often behavioural (boredom or separation anxiety) rather than medical. Identifying which category your dog falls into changes the entire treatment approach.

Signs to Watch For

  • Hair loss over one specific spot, usually the front paw or wrist
  • Red, inflamed, or raised thickened skin
  • Constant or repetitive licking at the same site
  • Open sores or wet, weeping wounds in advanced cases
  • The dog resists you touching the area

Myth vs Fact

MythFact
It's just a habit — it will go away on its ownUntreated lick granulomas typically worsen and can develop deep bacterial infection requiring long-term antibiotics
An E-collar alone solves the problemAn E-collar stops the licking mechanically but does not address the underlying cause — it will resume once removed unless the trigger is treated
Bitter-tasting sprays are a reliable fixMost dogs adapt to bitter sprays within days; they rarely resolve moderate-to-severe cases alone

Treatment

  • Identify the underlying cause — allergy testing, joint assessment, or a behavioural history, depending on the case
  • Medication — antibiotics if infection is present; anti-inflammatories or anti-anxiety medication where appropriate
  • E-collar or protective wrap — to break the physical licking cycle while the skin heals
  • Behavioural enrichment — increased exercise, puzzle feeders, and structured attention for boredom-driven cases
  • Allergy management — dietary trial or environmental control if allergy is the trigger
⚠️ Contact a veterinarian immediately if you notice: an open wound that isn't healing, a foul smell from the site, visible tendon or bone, or the dog becoming lethargic or feverish. These suggest a deep infection that needs prompt treatment.

Prevention

Daily exercise, mental stimulation (puzzle toys, training sessions), consistent parasite prevention, and regular veterinary check-ups all reduce the risk of lick granulomas forming in the first place. If your dog has a history of anxiety, addressing it early — before a lick spot forms — is far easier than treating an established one.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can lick granulomas heal completely?
Yes, with consistent treatment of the underlying cause. Chronic, long-standing cases take longer and may leave a permanent bald patch or scar.

Is this condition painful?
Yes — the thickened skin and any underlying infection are uncomfortable, which is part of why dogs continue to lick.

Which breeds are most prone to lick granulomas?
Large, energetic breeds such as Labradors, Great Danes, and German Shepherds are commonly affected, often linked to under-stimulation.

How long does treatment usually take?
Mild cases can improve in 2–3 weeks. Chronic, deep granulomas may take months of consistent management.

Should I stop my dog from licking immediately?
Yes — using an E-collar or bandage to interrupt the cycle while you address the root cause speeds healing significantly.

Can food allergies really cause a dog to lick its paw?
Yes. Paw licking is one of the most common signs of food or environmental allergy in dogs.

Will surgery ever be needed?
Rarely, and only for very severe, non-responsive cases with significant tissue damage. Most cases resolve with medical and behavioural management.

Can this happen to cats too?
Cats can develop similar over-grooming lesions, though acral lick dermatitis specifically is far more common in dogs.

If allergies are suspected, our clinical medicine team can help identify triggers. For dogs with joint-related licking, read about hip dysplasia and joint pain in dogs.

bird-feather-dna-sexing-test.title: Bird Feather DNA Sexing Test in Pune — Accurate Gender Testing for Parrots & Budgies
bird-feather-dna-sexing-test.summary: Can't tell if your bird is male or female? Feather DNA sexing gives 99%+ accurate results in 7-10 days without a blood draw. Learn how the test works at Shivraj Pet Clinic, Wakad & Pimple Saudagar, Pune.
bird-feather-dna-sexing-test.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine) — 24+ years of experience in companion animal and exotic pet medicine.

Most parrot species — African Greys, budgies, cockatiels, macaws, and lovebirds among them — are monomorphic, meaning males and females look identical to the naked eye. If you've ever guessed your bird's gender from behaviour alone and been wrong, you're not alone. At Shivraj Pet Clinic & Exotic Animal Centre, Wakad & Pimple Saudagar, Pune, feather DNA sexing is the test we recommend whenever certainty actually matters — breeding, pairing, or simply settling the debate at home.

Quick Facts

Species testedParrots, budgies, cockatiels, lovebirds, macaws, most companion bird species
Sample needed5–6 chest feathers with intact follicles
Turnaround time7–10 days
Accuracy99%+ when sample is collected correctly
InvasivenessMinimal — no blood draw, no sedation required

What Is Feather DNA Sexing?

Feather DNA sexing is a laboratory test that determines a bird's genetic sex by analysing DNA extracted from the base of freshly plucked feathers — specifically the follicle, the living tissue at the root. Unlike surgical sexing (which requires anaesthesia and an endoscope), this method is non-invasive and can be done during a routine clinic visit.

Why It Matters

  • Breeding management — you cannot pair birds responsibly without knowing their sex
  • Behavioural understanding — hormonal behaviours in birds (nesting, aggression, egg-laying) are sex-linked
  • Health planning — female birds carry unique risks such as egg binding that males don't; knowing sex shapes preventive care
  • Legal and pedigree documentation — some breed registries and export processes require confirmed sex
💡 In species like African Greys, cockatiels, and most macaws, visual sexing is unreliable even for experienced bird owners. DNA testing is the only method that removes guesswork entirely.

How the Test Works

  1. Feather collection — we pluck 5–6 chest feathers with follicles attached (a brief, well-tolerated procedure)
  2. Sample packaging — feathers are sealed and sent to a certified genetics lab
  3. DNA analysis — the lab examines sex chromosomes (birds use a ZZ/ZW system, opposite to mammals)
  4. Results — accurate male/female determination delivered within 7–10 days

Myth vs Fact

MythFact
You can tell a bird's sex from its behaviourBehaviour is influenced by hormones and personality, not a reliable sex indicator in monomorphic species
DNA sexing requires a blood drawFeather-based sampling is standard and equally accurate, without the stress of a blood draw
Pelvic bone spacing tells you the sexThis old method is unreliable in most parrot species and not recommended
⚠️ Never pull feathers yourself at home. Incorrect plucking can damage the follicle, cause bleeding, or give the lab an unusable sample — requiring a second, avoidable procedure.

Benefits of Feather DNA Sexing

  • Highly accurate (99%+) when performed correctly
  • Minimally invasive — no sedation, no surgery
  • Suitable for chicks as young as a few weeks old
  • One-time test — a bird's genetic sex never changes

Frequently Asked Questions

At what age can a bird be DNA sexed?
Feathers can be collected as soon as a chick has grown in its first chest feathers, typically a few weeks after hatching.

Does the test hurt the bird?
There is brief, momentary discomfort during feather collection, similar to what a bird experiences during normal moulting.

Can I use a moulted feather I found in the cage?
No. Moulted feathers have no living follicle tissue and cannot be used for DNA extraction.

Is this test available for all bird species?
It works for the vast majority of companion bird species. Ask us to confirm for less common species.

How much does feather DNA sexing cost?
Pricing depends on the lab and species. Call us for a current quote.

What if the result is inconclusive?
This is rare with a properly collected sample. If it happens, we recollect at no additional clinic charge.

Can DNA sexing detect health problems too?
No — it is specifically a sex-determination test, not a general health panel. Pair it with a wellness exam for full health screening.

Do I need to fast my bird before the test?
No fasting is required for feather collection.

complete-diet-guide-turtles-tortoises.title: Complete Diet Guide for Pet Turtles & Tortoises — Feeding Ratios & Safe Foods
complete-diet-guide-turtles-tortoises.summary: Improper diet is a leading cause of shell deformities and metabolic bone disease in turtles and tortoises. Get species-specific feeding ratios and safe foods from Shivraj Pet Clinic, Pune.
complete-diet-guide-turtles-tortoises.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine) — 24+ years of experience in companion animal and exotic pet medicine.

Turtles and tortoises are often assumed to be low-maintenance pets — but their dietary needs are precise, and getting them wrong has serious long-term consequences. At Shivraj Pet Clinic & Exotic Animal Centre, Wakad & Pimple Saudagar, Pune, improper nutrition is one of the most common underlying causes behind the shell and bone problems we treat.

Quick Facts

Species coveredAquatic turtles and land tortoises
Severity of poor dietCan cause permanent shell deformity and metabolic bone disease
Key nutrientCalcium-to-phosphorus ratio and UVB exposure for Vitamin D3 synthesis
Foods to avoidBread, dairy, processed foods, avocado, excessive spinach
PreventionSpecies-specific diet plus proper UVB lighting

Why Diet Matters

Improper nutrition contributes directly to metabolic bone disease (a weakening and softening of the shell and skeleton), shell deformities, obesity, and kidney disease. Because turtles and tortoises grow slowly, dietary mistakes often don't show visible effects for months — by the time deformity is visible, the damage may already be permanent.
