Pellets (complete aquatic turtle formula)40–50%
Leafy greens20–25%
Aquatic plants10–15%
Protein (fish, insects)15–20%
FruitUnder 5%

Tortoise Diet

Food GroupPercentage of Diet
Leafy greens70–80%
Vegetables15–20%
Edible flowers (hibiscus, nasturtium)5–10%
FruitUnder 5%
💡 The single most important factor for shell and bone health isn't food alone — it's the calcium-to-phosphorus ratio combined with adequate UVB lighting, which allows the body to actually use the calcium in the diet. A perfect diet under poor lighting still leads to metabolic bone disease.

Foods to Avoid

❌ Bread • Dairy products • Processed human food • Avocado • Excessive spinach (binds calcium) • Iceberg lettuce (little nutritional value) • Canned pet food not formulated for reptiles

Myth vs Fact

MythFact
Lettuce is a good staple food for tortoisesIceberg lettuce is mostly water with minimal nutrition — dark leafy greens are far better staples
Fruit should make up a large part of the dietFruit should be under 5% of the diet — too much causes digestive upset and imbalanced nutrition
If they're growing, the diet must be fineTurtles can grow in size while still developing metabolic bone disease — growth alone isn't proof of good nutrition
⚠️ Contact a veterinarian if you notice a soft or flexible shell, visible shell deformity, lethargy, or reluctance to eat — these can indicate metabolic bone disease or an underlying nutritional deficiency that needs correction.

Calcium and Supplementation

Most captive turtles and tortoises benefit from calcium supplementation (calcium powder dusted on food), especially growing juveniles and egg-laying females. Cuttlebone is a convenient, self-regulating calcium source for many species. Ask us for a species-specific supplementation schedule.

Frequently Asked Questions

How often should I feed my turtle or tortoise?
Juveniles typically need daily feeding; adults often do well with feeding every 1–2 days, depending on species. We can advise based on your pet's age and species.

Can I feed my tortoise fruit every day?
No — fruit should stay under 5% of the diet and is best offered as an occasional treat, not a daily staple.

Do all species need the same calcium supplementation?
No — requirements vary by species, age, and whether the female is reproductively active. Ask us for specifics.

Is tap water safe for aquatic turtles?
Tap water is generally fine once dechlorinated; ask us about appropriate water conditioning for your setup.

What's the biggest dietary mistake you see?
Feeding a diet too high in fruit and too low in calcium-rich greens, combined with inadequate UVB lighting.

Can diet alone prevent metabolic bone disease?
No — diet must be paired with proper UVB lighting for calcium to be metabolised effectively.

Are commercial pellets enough on their own?
Pellets are a good base but should be combined with fresh greens and, for aquatic species, some protein — not fed exclusively.

My tortoise refuses vegetables — what should I do?
This can indicate a health issue or simply pickiness developed from an early diet too high in fruit. Bring your tortoise in for an assessment.

If you notice shell softness or unusual growth, our turtle health guide and Exotic Animal Centre services can help.

Species-specific diets plus correct UVB lighting are essential for lifelong shell health. Book a consultation at Shivraj Pet Clinic, Wakad & Pimple Saudagar, Pune.

dental-scaling-dogs-cats.title: Professional Dental Scaling for Dogs & Cats in Pune — Why It Matters
dental-scaling-dogs-cats.summary: Over 80% of dogs and 70% of cats develop dental disease by age 3. Learn why professional dental scaling under anaesthesia protects your pet's oral and overall health — Shivraj Pet Clinic, Pune.
dental-scaling-dogs-cats.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine) — 24+ years of experience in companion animal and exotic pet medicine.

Over 80% of dogs and 70% of cats develop some form of dental disease by the age of 3 — yet dental health remains one of the most overlooked aspects of pet care. At Shivraj Pet Clinic, Wakad & Pimple Saudagar, Pune, we perform professional dental scaling and oral health assessments to prevent pain, tooth loss, and the serious systemic disease that dental infection can cause.

Quick Facts

Species affectedDogs and cats (small breeds especially prone)
Prevalence80%+ of dogs, 70%+ of cats by age 3
ProcedurePerformed under general anaesthesia with pre-anaesthetic bloodwork
Recommended frequencyEvery 1–3 years depending on breed and home care
Emergency signsFacial swelling, refusal to eat, severe bleeding gums

Why Dental Health Matters

Dental disease is not just about bad breath. When bacteria accumulate in the mouth and form tartar (hardened calculus), they can enter the bloodstream and cause:

  • Heart valve disease — bacteria settling on heart valves
  • Kidney damage — chronic low-grade infection taxes kidney filtration
  • Liver disease — bacterial toxins processed by the liver
  • Chronic pain — loose, infected teeth cause constant discomfort that pets hide

Dogs and cats do not show pain the way humans do. A pet with severe dental disease often continues eating — right up until they cannot.

🔍 Clinical insight: At Shivraj Pet Clinic, we frequently see pet parents surprised at how much brighter and more energetic their pet becomes after a long-overdue dental scaling — chronic oral pain is often mistaken for "just getting older."

Signs Your Pet Needs Dental Attention

  • Bad breath (beyond normal "dog breath")
  • Yellow or brown deposits on teeth near the gum line
  • Red, swollen, or bleeding gums
  • Loose teeth
  • Drooling more than usual
  • Pawing at the mouth
  • Preference for soft food or dropping food while eating
  • Facial swelling under the eye (often indicates a tooth root abscess)

Myth vs Fact

MythFact
Anaesthesia-free dentistry is a safer alternativeA conscious pet cannot hold still for sub-gingival (below gum line) cleaning, where disease actually lives — it is cosmetic only and can miss serious disease
Bad breath is just normal for petsPersistent bad breath is one of the most reliable early signs of dental disease, not a normal trait
Dry food alone keeps teeth cleanDry food provides only mild mechanical cleaning; it does not replace brushing or professional scaling

The Dental Scaling Procedure

Professional dental scaling at Shivraj Pet Clinic involves:

  1. Pre-anaesthetic bloodwork — essential before general anaesthesia
  2. General anaesthesia — pets must be fully anaesthetised for thorough and safe scaling
  3. Scaling — ultrasonic and hand instruments remove tartar from all tooth surfaces
  4. Probing — checking for periodontal pockets and loose teeth
  5. Extraction — severely diseased teeth are extracted rather than left to cause ongoing pain and infection
  6. Polishing — smooths enamel to slow future tartar accumulation
⚠️ Contact us promptly if you notice facial swelling, sudden refusal to eat, or heavy bleeding from the gums — these can indicate an advanced tooth root abscess needing urgent attention.

Maintaining Oral Health at Home

  • Tooth brushing — daily brushing with pet-safe toothpaste is the gold standard. Start slowly, let your pet lick the toothpaste first, introduce the brush gradually
  • Dental chews — those with the VOHC (Veterinary Oral Health Council) seal have evidence behind them
  • Dental diets — certain prescription diets help reduce tartar mechanically
  • Water additives — some products reduce bacterial counts in drinking water

Professional dental scaling is typically needed every 1–3 years depending on your pet's breed and oral hygiene routine. Small breeds (Shih Tzu, Dachshund, Pomeranians) tend to develop tartar faster and may need annual scaling.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is dental scaling safe for older pets?
Yes, with proper pre-anaesthetic screening. Age alone is not a reason to avoid necessary dental care — untreated dental disease is often the greater risk.

How long does the procedure take?
Typically 30–60 minutes depending on the extent of tartar and whether extractions are needed.

Will my pet need to stay overnight?
Most pets go home the same day, once fully recovered from anaesthesia.

How can I tell if my pet is in dental pain?
Pets rarely show obvious pain — watch for subtle signs like reduced chewing on one side, reluctance to play with toys, or reduced interest in hard treats.

Do cats need dental scaling as much as dogs?
Yes — cats develop dental disease at similarly high rates and often show fewer obvious signs, making regular checks important.

Can I prevent the need for scaling with brushing alone?
Regular brushing significantly reduces tartar buildup and can extend the time between professional scalings, but it does not eliminate the need entirely.

What happens if dental disease is left untreated?
Progressive tooth loss, chronic pain, and increased risk of the bacteria affecting the heart, kidneys, and liver.

Is anaesthesia safe for my pet?
We use modern anaesthesia protocols with pre-anaesthetic bloodwork and continuous monitoring, the same standard used in human hospitals.

Our preventive medicine service can help build a full oral care plan alongside routine wellness checks.

Professional dental scaling protects both oral and overall health. Book a dental assessment at Shivraj Pet Clinic, Wakad & Pimple Saudagar, Pune, or call 077569 65169.

ear-infections-dogs.title: Ear Infections in Dogs — Signs, Causes & Treatment in Pune
ear-infections-dogs.summary: Head shaking, scratching, and bad odour are classic signs of a dog ear infection. Learn the causes, treatment, and how to prevent recurrence from Shivraj Pet Clinic, Wakad & Pimple Saudagar, Pune.
ear-infections-dogs.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine) — 24+ years of experience in companion animal and exotic pet medicine.

Ear infections are among the most common — and most uncomfortable — problems we see at Shivraj Pet Clinic, Wakad & Pimple Saudagar, Pune. They're especially frequent in floppy-eared breeds and during Pune's humid monsoon months, when moisture gets trapped in the ear canal and bacteria or yeast multiply rapidly.

Quick Facts

Species affectedDogs (all breeds; floppy-eared breeds at higher risk)
SeverityMild to severe — untreated infections can spread to the middle/inner ear
Common causesBacteria, yeast, ear mites, allergies, trapped moisture
Emergency signsHead tilt, loss of balance, severe pain, swelling of the ear flap
PreventionKeep ears dry, routine cleaning, allergy management

Why Ear Health Matters

A dog's ear canal is L-shaped and deeper than a human's, which makes it excellent at trapping moisture, wax, and debris. Left unaddressed, infections cause real pain — dogs with ear infections often become irritable or withdrawn simply because the discomfort is constant.

Signs of an Ear Infection

  • Head shaking or tilting
  • Scratching or pawing at the ear
  • Foul odour from the ear canal
  • Discharge — brown, yellow, or bloody
  • Redness or swelling inside the ear flap
  • Sensitivity or pain when the ear is touched
  • Rubbing the ear against furniture or the floor
🔍 Clinical insight: At Shivraj Pet Clinic, we see a sharp rise in ear infections every monsoon season — particularly in Labradors, Cocker Spaniels, and Beagles. Owners often mistake early head-shaking for a minor irritation and delay the visit, which allows a simple case to progress into a painful, harder-to-treat one.

Causes

  • Bacteria and yeast — the most common causes, often triggered by excess moisture
  • Ear mites — more common in puppies, highly contagious between pets
  • Allergies — food or environmental allergies frequently show up first as recurring ear infections
  • Excess moisture — from swimming, bathing, or humid weather
  • Foreign bodies — grass seeds or debris lodged in the canal

Myth vs Fact

MythFact
A dog's ear infection will clear up on its ownMost ear infections worsen without treatment and can spread deeper into the ear, risking permanent hearing damage
Any home oil or remedy is safe to pour into the earUnapproved home remedies can worsen infection or cause damage if the eardrum is compromised — always use vet-approved products
Only floppy-eared dogs get ear infectionsAll breeds can be affected; floppy ears simply trap more moisture, increasing risk

Treatment

Treatment starts with a proper examination — we use an otoscope to check the eardrum and identify whether the cause is bacterial, yeast, mite-related, or a combination. Based on findings:

  • Professional ear cleaning to remove debris and discharge
  • Medicated drops targeted to the specific cause (antibiotic, antifungal, or anti-parasitic)
  • Oral medication for severe or recurrent infections
  • Treatment of the underlying cause — for example, an allergy management plan if infections keep recurring
⚠️ Contact us immediately if your dog shows a head tilt, loss of balance, circling, or sudden severe pain — these can indicate the infection has spread to the middle or inner ear, which requires urgent treatment.

Prevention

  • Dry your dog's ears thoroughly after baths or swimming
  • Clean ears weekly with a vet-approved cleaner — never cotton buds deep in the canal
  • Check ears regularly if your dog has floppy or hairy ears
  • Address allergies early, since recurring infections are often allergy-driven

Frequently Asked Questions

How often should I clean my dog's ears?
Weekly for breeds prone to infections; every 2–3 weeks for others, or as advised after an infection.

Can I use human ear drops on my dog?
No. Always use veterinary-formulated products — human products can be ineffective or harmful.

Why does my dog keep getting the same infection back?
Recurring infections are frequently a sign of an underlying allergy that hasn't been addressed. Ask us about allergy testing.

Is ear infection contagious to other pets?
Bacterial and yeast infections generally aren't contagious, but ear mites are highly contagious between pets.

How long does treatment usually take?
Mild infections often clear in 1–2 weeks with proper treatment; chronic cases can take longer and need ongoing management.

Can I just clean the ear myself instead of visiting the vet?
Cleaning helps with prevention, but an active infection needs a proper diagnosis — treating blind risks masking a worsening problem.

Do certain foods cause ear infections?
Some food allergies (commonly chicken, beef, or dairy) can trigger inflammation that leads to ear infections. See our guide to food allergies in dogs.

What breeds are most at risk in Pune's climate?
Labradors, Cocker Spaniels, Beagles, and other floppy or hairy-eared breeds see the highest rates, especially during monsoon.

If allergies may be contributing, our clinical medicine service can help identify the trigger. Persistent ear infections need veterinary care — early treatment reduces pain and prevents complications.

Book a consultation at Shivraj Pet Clinic, Wakad & Pimple Saudagar, Pune, or call 077569 65169.

hair-fall-dogs-cats.title: Hair Fall in Dogs & Cats — When Is Shedding Normal vs a Medical Problem?
hair-fall-dogs-cats.summary: Seasonal shedding is normal — patchy bald spots or sudden hair loss are not. Learn the causes, diagnosis, and treatment for excessive hair fall in dogs and cats at Shivraj Pet Clinic, Pune.
hair-fall-dogs-cats.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine) — 24+ years of experience in companion animal and exotic pet medicine.

Every dog and cat sheds — it's a normal part of the hair growth cycle. But when shedding turns into patchy bald spots, thinning fur, or hair loss accompanied by itching and irritated skin, it's usually a sign of an underlying issue. At Shivraj Pet Clinic, Wakad & Pimple Saudagar, Pune, hair fall is one of the most common reasons pet parents bring their dogs and cats in for a skin consultation.

Quick Facts

Species affectedDogs and cats
SeverityRanges from cosmetic to a sign of significant internal illness
Common causesAllergies, fleas/ticks, hormonal disorders, nutritional deficiency, stress
Emergency signsRapid, severe hair loss with lethargy or weight change
PreventionParasite prevention, balanced diet, regular grooming, early diagnosis

Normal vs Excessive Hair Loss

Seasonal shedding — typically heavier in spring and autumn — is completely normal and usually even across the coat. What's not normal: patchy bald areas, hair loss concentrated in one spot, accompanying itching or redness, or shedding so severe you can see the skin clearly through the coat.

Common Causes

  • Allergies — food or environmental allergies causing itching and secondary hair loss from scratching
  • Fleas and ticks — parasite bites trigger intense itching, especially at the base of the tail and around the neck
  • Hormonal disorders — thyroid disease and other endocrine conditions frequently present first as coat changes
  • Nutritional deficiencies — an unbalanced diet directly affects coat quality and growth
  • Stress — cats in particular can over-groom to the point of hair loss when stressed or anxious
  • Fungal infection (ringworm) — causes circular patches of hair loss, and is transmissible to humans
🔍 Clinical insight: At Shivraj Pet Clinic, we frequently find that "hair loss" cases owners assume are skin problems are actually early signs of a hormonal or nutritional issue. A proper diagnostic work-up — not just a topical treatment — is what actually resolves these cases long-term.

Myth vs Fact

MythFact
Hair loss is always just a skin problemIt's frequently a sign of an internal issue — hormonal imbalance, allergy, or nutritional deficiency
Shaving a shedding pet reduces future sheddingShaving does not reduce the shedding cycle and can affect the coat's ability to regulate temperature and protect skin
Cats don't get allergies the way dogs doCats absolutely develop food and environmental allergies, often showing up as over-grooming and hair loss rather than obvious itching

Veterinary Diagnosis

Because so many different conditions cause hair loss, an accurate diagnosis usually requires more than a visual check:

  • Skin scraping — checks for mites and parasites under the microscope
  • Blood tests — screens for thyroid and other hormonal imbalances
  • Fungal testing — identifies ringworm and other fungal causes
  • Dietary evaluation — reviews current nutrition for gaps or trigger ingredients
⚠️ Contact a veterinarian promptly if hair loss is sudden and severe, accompanied by lethargy, appetite changes, or weight change — these can indicate a significant underlying illness, not just a skin condition.

Home Care

  • Regular grooming to distribute natural skin oils and reduce matting
  • A balanced, high-quality diet appropriate for your pet's life stage
  • Consistent parasite prevention year-round, not just during monsoon
  • Follow-up care as directed once an underlying cause is identified and treated

Frequently Asked Questions

Is it normal for cats to over-groom?
Occasional grooming is normal, but grooming to the point of visible bald patches usually signals stress, allergy, or a medical issue.

Can diet really cause hair loss?
Yes — deficiencies in essential fatty acids and protein directly affect coat quality and can cause thinning or dull, brittle fur.

How do I know if it's fleas or something else?
Fleas usually cause hair loss concentrated at the tail base, neck, and groin, often with visible flea dirt in the coat. Other causes tend to be more evenly distributed or patchy elsewhere.

Is ringworm dangerous to humans?
Yes — ringworm is zoonotic and can spread to people, especially children. Prompt treatment and hygiene precautions are important.

Will hair grow back after treatment?
In most cases, yes, once the underlying cause is treated. Hormonal cases may take several months to show full regrowth.

Can stress alone cause hair loss in cats?
Yes — psychogenic over-grooming from stress or anxiety is a recognised and treatable cause of hair loss in cats.

Should I change my pet's food if I see hair loss?
Only after veterinary guidance — an elimination diet trial should be structured properly, not guessed at home.

How long does diagnosis usually take?
Simple cases (like fleas) are diagnosed at the first visit. Hormonal or allergy causes may need blood work or a longer diet trial to confirm.

If your pet's hair loss comes with persistent itching, our clinical medicine team can help identify the cause. For dogs specifically prone to allergy-driven skin issues, see our guide on food allergies in dogs.

Healthy skin starts with early diagnosis. Book a consultation at Shivraj Pet Clinic, Wakad & Pimple Saudagar, Pune if your pet's shedding becomes excessive.

non-surgical-heat-management-cats.title: Non-Surgical Heat Control in Cats — Temporary Options & Why Spaying Still Wins
non-surgical-heat-management-cats.summary: Can a cat's heat cycle be managed without surgery? Yes, but only temporarily and under veterinary supervision. Learn the real options and risks from Shivraj Pet Clinic, Wakad & Pimple Saudagar, Pune.
non-surgical-heat-management-cats.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine) — 24+ years of experience in companion animal and exotic pet medicine.

Not every pet parent is ready to spay immediately — breeding plans, a very young cat, or a temporary situation can all be valid reasons to ask about alternatives. At Shivraj Pet Clinic, Wakad & Pimple Saudagar, Pune, we get this question often: can heat be managed without surgery? The honest answer is yes, but only as a short-term, supervised measure — not a long-term substitute for spaying.

If you're not yet sure whether your cat is actually in heat, start with our guide on recognising the signs of heat in cats and dogs before deciding on a management approach.

Quick Facts

Applies toFemale cats not yet spayed
Can heat be stopped without surgery?Temporarily, under veterinary supervision only
Main risk of repeated useSignificantly increased risk of pyometra and mammary tumours
Recommended long-term solutionSpaying
Never useHuman hormone tablets, herbal remedies, sedatives, alcohol

Can Heat Be Controlled Without Surgery?

Yes — but only temporarily, and always under veterinary supervision. There is no safe, effective way to permanently manage a cat's reproductive cycle without eventually addressing it surgically or medically through proper veterinary channels.

Non-Surgical Options

  • Hormonal medications — short-term use only, prescribed and monitored by a vet; not intended for repeated or long-term use
  • GnRH implants — availability varies by region and product; these suppress the cycle for a defined period under veterinary guidance
  • Environmental management — keeping a cat strictly indoors and away from intact males reduces unwanted breeding risk, though it does not stop the heat cycle itself
🔍 Clinical insight: At Shivraj Pet Clinic, the cats we see most often in emergency for pyometra (a life-threatening uterine infection) have a history of repeated hormonal suppression rather than spaying. The short-term convenience carries a real long-term cost.

Myth vs Fact

MythFact
Hormone injections are a safe long-term alternative to spayingRepeated hormonal suppression significantly raises the risk of pyometra and mammary tumours over time
Herbal or home remedies can safely suppress heatNo herbal remedy has proven safety or efficacy for this purpose — some can be actively harmful
A cat needs to have one litter before spayingThere is no medical benefit to letting a cat have a litter first; spaying before the first heat carries the lowest long-term health risk

What to Avoid

❌ Human hormone tablets • Herbal remedies of unproven safety • Sedatives used to "calm" heat behaviour • Alcohol or other home remedies circulating online

⚠️ Never administer human medication, sedatives, or unverified herbal products to suppress your cat's heat. These are not evaluated for feline safety and can cause serious harm.

Why Spaying Is Still the Best Long-Term Option

Spaying permanently prevents unwanted pregnancies and significantly reduces the risk of pyometra and mammary tumours — risks that increase with every unmanaged heat cycle. It also eliminates the behavioural stress of repeated heat cycles for both the cat and the household.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is it safe to use hormonal medication just once?
A single, vet-supervised use for a specific short-term situation carries far less risk than repeated or ongoing use — but it should always be discussed with your vet first.

At what age can I spay my cat?
We generally recommend spaying by 5–6 months, ideally before the first heat cycle.

Does letting a cat go through heat without mating cause harm?
Repeated unmanaged cycles over a long period do increase reproductive health risks over time, even without mating.

Can indoor-only cats still go into heat?
Yes — heat cycles occur regardless of indoor or outdoor lifestyle, though indoor cats have a much lower unwanted pregnancy risk.

Are GnRH implants available in Pune?
Availability varies — ask us during a consultation about current options.

What are the signs my cat needs emergency care during heat management?
Lethargy, loss of appetite, vomiting, or abdominal swelling need immediate attention, particularly in cats with a history of hormonal suppression.

Is spaying safe for an older cat?
Yes, with proper pre-surgical assessment — age alone isn't a barrier, though risk factors are evaluated individually.

How soon after using hormonal medication can I schedule spaying?
This depends on the specific medication used — we'll advise timing during your consultation.

Consult Shivraj Pet Clinic, Wakad & Pimple Saudagar, Pune to discuss the safest option for your cat — book a consultation or call 077569 65169.

respiratory-infections-pet-turtles.title: Respiratory Infections in Pet Turtles — Symptoms, Causes & Treatment in Pune
respiratory-infections-pet-turtles.summary: Wheezing, open-mouth breathing, or nasal discharge in a pet turtle can signal a life-threatening respiratory infection. Learn the causes and treatment from Shivraj Pet Clinic, Wakad & Pimple Saudagar, Pune.
respiratory-infections-pet-turtles.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine) — 24+ years of experience in companion animal and exotic pet medicine.

Turtles are excellent at masking illness — by the time a respiratory infection becomes visible, it's often already advanced. At Shivraj Pet Clinic & Exotic Animal Centre, Wakad & Pimple Saudagar, Pune, we regularly treat turtles and tortoises with respiratory disease, most often traced back to incorrect temperature or lighting at home.

Quick Facts

Species affectedAquatic turtles, tortoises, and other reptiles
SeverityCan be life-threatening without timely treatment
Common causesCold temperatures, poor UVB lighting, dirty water, stress
Emergency signsOpen-mouth breathing, wheezing, complete loss of appetite
PreventionCorrect temperature, UVB lighting, clean water, balanced diet

Why Respiratory Infections Are Serious in Turtles

Unlike mammals, reptiles have a slower metabolism and a less obvious way of showing distress. A turtle with a respiratory infection can continue to appear "fine" to an untrained eye right up until the infection becomes critical. Left untreated, respiratory infections can progress to pneumonia and become life-threatening.

Symptoms to Watch For

  • Wheezing or clicking sounds when breathing
  • Nasal or ocular discharge
  • Open-mouth breathing or gasping
  • Lethargy and reduced activity
  • Loss of appetite
  • Floating unevenly or tilted to one side in water (buoyancy problems, common with lung involvement)
🔍 Clinical insight: At Shivraj Pet Clinic, the vast majority of respiratory infections we treat in pet turtles trace back to one root cause — incorrect basking temperature. A turtle kept even a few degrees too cool cannot mount a proper immune response, making infection far more likely.

Causes

  • Cold temperatures — inadequate basking spot temperature suppresses the immune system
  • Poor UVB lighting — insufficient UVB affects overall immune health and calcium metabolism
  • Dirty or poorly filtered water — harbours bacteria that can enter through the nose and mouth
  • Stress — overcrowding, poor handling, or an unsuitable enclosure size

Myth vs Fact

MythFact
Turtles don't need special heating — room temperature is fineTurtles require a specific basking temperature gradient; room temperature alone is almost always too cold and suppresses immunity
A turtle that's still eating can't have a respiratory infectionTurtles often continue eating even with a developing infection — appetite alone isn't a reliable health indicator
Bubbles from the nose are normalNasal bubbling or discharge is a common early sign of respiratory infection and should be checked promptly

Treatment

  • Veterinary antibiotics — prescribed based on examination and, where needed, diagnostic testing
  • Habitat correction — adjusting basking temperature, water temperature, and UVB lighting to species-appropriate levels
  • Supportive care — fluid therapy and nutritional support for turtles not eating well
  • Warm, dry recovery environment — for aquatic species, this may mean limiting time in water during treatment
⚠️ Contact a veterinarian immediately if your turtle shows open-mouth breathing, wheezing, or has stopped eating for more than a couple of days. Respiratory infections in reptiles can progress quickly to pneumonia.

Prevention

  • Maintain the correct basking and water temperature for your turtle's species
  • Provide proper UVB lighting, replaced on schedule as bulbs lose effectiveness over time
  • Keep water clean with adequate filtration and regular water changes
  • Feed a balanced, species-appropriate diet to support overall immune health

Frequently Asked Questions

What temperature should my turtle's basking spot be?
This varies by species — ask us for a species-specific temperature and lighting guide during your visit.

Can respiratory infections be cured completely?
Yes, with prompt treatment and habitat correction. Delayed treatment significantly reduces the chances of full recovery.

Is this contagious to other turtles?
Some respiratory pathogens can spread between reptiles, so isolating a sick turtle from tank-mates is recommended until cleared by a vet.

My turtle is still swimming normally — could it still be sick?
Yes. Early respiratory infections can be present before obvious swimming or buoyancy changes appear.

How is a respiratory infection diagnosed?
Through physical examination, and where needed, imaging or laboratory testing to identify the specific cause.

Can poor diet contribute to respiratory illness?
Yes — nutritional deficiencies, particularly Vitamin A deficiency, weaken the respiratory tract's natural defences. See our turtle and tortoise diet guide.

How often should I check my turtle's habitat setup?
Check basking temperature and UVB bulb function regularly — UVB output declines over months even if the bulb still lights up.

Do land tortoises get respiratory infections too?
Yes, tortoises are equally susceptible, usually linked to cold, damp housing conditions.

Explore our Exotic Animal Centre for full reptile care services, including habitat consultations.

Early veterinary care significantly improves recovery. Book a consultation at Shivraj Pet Clinic, Wakad & Pimple Saudagar, Pune, or call 077569 65169.

dog-losing-weight-despite-eating.title: Why Is My Dog Losing Weight Despite Eating Normally?
dog-losing-weight-despite-eating.summary: Weight loss in a dog that's still eating normally can point to underlying illness. Learn the possible causes and why this symptom shouldn't be ignored.
dog-losing-weight-despite-eating.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

A dog eating normally but still losing weight is a genuinely confusing symptom for owners — the intuitive logic of "eating fine means healthy" doesn't hold here, and that gap is exactly why it needs investigation.

Why This Combination Is a Red Flag

Weight loss despite normal or even increased appetite suggests the body isn't properly absorbing or using nutrients — rather than a simple case of not eating enough.

Possible Causes

Intestinal parasites, malabsorption disorders, diabetes, hyperthyroidism (less common in dogs than cats but possible), chronic organ disease, and certain cancers can all present this way.

What to Track and Report

Note how long the weight loss has been happening, whether appetite has actually increased, decreased, or stayed the same, and any other changes — energy level, thirst, stool consistency, coat quality. This history significantly speeds up diagnosis.

Diagnosis Approach

A physical exam and weight history are the starting point, typically followed by bloodwork, fecal testing for parasites, and imaging if a structural cause is suspected.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much weight loss is significant?
Any noticeable, unintentional weight loss over weeks is worth investigating rather than waiting to see if it continues.

Could this be from increased activity or a diet change?
It's possible, but if the dog's routine and diet haven't changed and weight loss continues, an underlying cause should be ruled out.

Is this more common in older dogs?
Some causes — chronic organ disease, certain cancers — are more common in seniors, but the symptom warrants evaluation at any age.

Can parasites really cause significant weight loss?
Yes, particularly in cases of heavy parasite burden, which is why fecal testing is a standard part of the workup.

⚠️ If you notice these signs in your pet, don't wait it out at home.

Call Shivraj Pet Clinic & Lab at 077569 65169 or book an appointment online — we serve pet parents across Pimple Nilakh, Wakad, Pimple Saudagar, and Vishal Nagar, with same-visit lab results and full diagnostic support under one roof.

nutritional-deficiencies-pet-parrots.title: Common Nutritional Deficiencies in Pet Parrots
nutritional-deficiencies-pet-parrots.summary: An all-seed diet is behind many common parrot health problems. Learn the most frequent nutritional deficiencies and how to correct them.
nutritional-deficiencies-pet-parrots.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

Nutritional deficiency remains one of the most preventable, and most common, root causes of chronic illness in companion parrots — almost always tracing back to an unbalanced, seed-heavy diet.

Vitamin A Deficiency

Among the most common deficiencies, showing up as poor feather quality, increased infection risk, and changes around the beak and skin.

Calcium Deficiency

Can affect bone health and egg-laying hens in particular, often linked to diets low in calcium-rich foods.

The Fix

A species-appropriate, formulated diet with fresh vegetables — not seeds alone — addresses most common deficiencies over time.

Frequently Asked Questions

Are all-seed diets really that risky?
Yes, they're one of the most common preventable causes of chronic illness in pet parrots.

Can supplements replace diet correction?
Diet correction is the primary fix; supplements should be used under veterinary guidance, not as a substitute.

How long does it take to correct a deficiency?
This varies by severity and requires veterinary guidance for a safe transition plan.

dog-vaccination-schedule-india.title: Complete Dog Vaccination Schedule in India: From Puppy DP to Annual Boosters
dog-vaccination-schedule-india.summary: A clear, age-by-age dog vaccination schedule for Indian pet owners — puppy shots, core vaccines, rabies timing, and annual boosters explained.
dog-vaccination-schedule-india.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

Vaccination confusion is one of the most common reasons puppies end up under-protected — not because owners don't care, but because schedules get missed, delayed, or misunderstood. Here's a straightforward, age-by-age breakdown of what a dog vaccination schedule in India typically looks like, and why timing matters as much as the vaccine itself.

Why Timing Matters

Puppies are born with some temporary immunity from their mother, which fades gradually over the first weeks of life. Vaccinating too early means the maternal antibodies can interfere with the vaccine; vaccinating too late leaves a gap where the puppy has no protection at all. This is why a structured, multi-dose schedule — not a single shot — is standard.

The Puppy Schedule

Generally, the first core vaccine (often called Puppy DP, covering Distemper and Parvovirus) is given around 6-8 weeks, with follow-up doses every 2-4 weeks until the puppy reaches roughly 16 weeks. The core combination (commonly DHPPi/DHLPPi) continues through this window, alongside the rabies vaccine, usually starting around 14-16 weeks.

Adult Boosters

Once the puppy series is complete, adult dogs move to a booster schedule — commonly annual for the core combination and leptospirosis, with rabies boosters following your local regulations (often every 1-3 years). Lifestyle vaccines like Bordetella (kennel cough) are added if your dog socializes frequently at parks, boarding, or grooming facilities.

💡 A rescued adult dog with unknown history, a puppy from a breeder with a partial vaccine record, and a dog boarding regularly all need different plans. At Shivraj Pet Clinic & Lab, we build the schedule around your dog's actual history and lifestyle rather than applying a single generic chart.

Frequently Asked Questions

My puppy missed a scheduled dose — do we start over?
Not usually — your vet can typically resume from where you left off, though the exact catch-up plan depends on how much time has passed.

Is the rabies vaccine legally required in India?
Rabies vaccination is strongly recommended and often required under local regulations; ask your vet about current requirements in your area.

Does an indoor dog need the full schedule?
Yes. Several core diseases spread through contaminated environments and objects, not just direct contact with other dogs, so indoor dogs still need protection.

When should adult boosters start?
Typically one year after the puppy series completes, then on an annual or multi-year cycle depending on the specific vaccine.

parrot-avian-vet-checkup-frequency.title: How Often Should a Pet Parrot See an Avian Veterinarian?
parrot-avian-vet-checkup-frequency.summary: Parrots hide illness well, making scheduled checkups more important than symptom-triggered visits alone. Here's a recommended frequency.
parrot-avian-vet-checkup-frequency.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

Because parrots are experts at masking illness, scheduled checkups matter more for this species than for most companion animals.

Recommended Frequency

An annual exam is generally recommended for healthy adult parrots, covering a physical exam and weight tracking.

Why Annual Isn't Always Enough

Given how well birds hide symptoms, some owners and vets opt for more frequent wellness visits, particularly for larger, longer-lived species.

Between Visits

Any change in droppings, appetite, activity, or feather condition warrants an unscheduled visit regardless of the last checkup date.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is annual enough for a healthy young parrot?
Generally yes, though your avian vet can advise based on species and individual history.

Do larger parrot species need different frequency?
Discuss with your vet — longer-lived species may benefit from closer monitoring over their lifespan.

What does a wellness exam include?
Typically a physical exam, weight check, and a review of diet and husbandry.

dog-fever-recognize-symptoms.title: Dog Fever: How to Recognize It and When a Vet Visit Is Necessary
dog-fever-recognize-symptoms.summary: A dog with a fever may seem lethargic, warm, or off their food. Learn how to recognize fever in dogs and when it needs veterinary attention.
dog-fever-recognize-symptoms.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

Dogs can't tell you they feel feverish, and a warm nose isn't a reliable indicator — recognizing fever in dogs takes knowing the actual signs, not the old myths.

Signs of Fever in Dogs

Lethargy, reduced appetite, shivering, warm ears and body, red or glassy-looking eyes, and reduced interest in usual activities are common signs. A warm, dry nose is not a reliable fever indicator on its own.

Taking Temperature Accurately

The only reliable way to confirm fever is a proper rectal temperature reading with a pet-appropriate thermometer. Guessing from touch alone is unreliable.

Common Causes

Infections (bacterial, viral, or from a wound), inflammation, recent vaccination (mild, short-lived fever is possible), and, less commonly, immune-mediated conditions can all cause fever.

When to See a Vet

A fever lasting more than a day, a very high reading, or fever accompanied by lethargy, vomiting, diarrhea, or refusal to eat should prompt a veterinary visit rather than home monitoring alone. Never give human fever medication (like paracetamol or ibuprofen) to a dog — these can be toxic.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is a dry nose a reliable sign of fever?
No — nose temperature and moisture vary for many reasons unrelated to fever and shouldn't be used to judge your dog's temperature.

Can I give my dog paracetamol for a fever?
No — human fever medications can be toxic to dogs. Always consult your vet for appropriate treatment.

Is a mild fever after vaccination normal?
A brief, mild fever can occur after vaccination and typically resolves within a day; a fever that persists or is accompanied by other symptoms should be checked.

What's considered a genuine emergency fever?
A very high temperature, or fever combined with lethargy, vomiting, or collapse, should be treated as urgent rather than monitored at home.

respiratory-diseases-pet-birds.title: Common Respiratory Diseases in Pet Birds
respiratory-diseases-pet-birds.summary: Respiratory disease is a leading cause of avian illness. Learn the common conditions and why birds are particularly vulnerable.
respiratory-diseases-pet-birds.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

Birds' unique respiratory anatomy — lungs plus air sacs — means respiratory disease affects them differently, and often more seriously, than mammals.

Why Birds Are Vulnerable

The efficient but delicate air-sac system means infections or irritants can spread and impact breathing capacity more significantly than in mammals.

Common Causes

Bacterial and fungal infections, nutritional deficiency (particularly Vitamin A), and environmental irritants like smoke or fumes are common contributors.

Recognizing It Early

Tail bobbing, open-mouth breathing, and voice changes are early signs worth acting on immediately, not monitoring.

Frequently Asked Questions

Are certain environments riskier for bird respiratory health?
Yes, smoke, aerosols, and certain cookware fumes are known risks.

Can diet affect respiratory disease risk?
Yes, Vitamin A deficiency specifically is linked to increased respiratory vulnerability.

Is respiratory disease in birds always an emergency?
Any visible respiratory distress should be treated as urgent given how quickly birds can decline.

tricat-vaccine-cats.title: Feline Care: Why the Tricat Vaccine Is Essential for Indoor and Outdoor Cats
tricat-vaccine-cats.summary: The Tricat (FVRCP) vaccine protects cats against three serious infectious diseases, including feline panleukopenia. Here's why indoor cats need it too.
tricat-vaccine-cats.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

“My cat never goes outside” is the single most common reason owners skip or delay the Tricat vaccine — and it's also the reasoning that leaves cats exposed to diseases that don't require outdoor contact to spread.

What Tricat Protects Against

The Tricat vaccine (also called FVRCP) protects against three significant feline diseases: feline viral rhinotracheitis, calicivirus, and feline panleukopenia. Panleukopenia in particular is a severe, often life-threatening disease that we cover in more depth elsewhere on this site.

Why Indoor Cats Still Need It

Viruses don't need your cat to go outside to reach them. They can travel in on shoes, clothing, a visitor's hands, a newly adopted animal, or a contaminated carrier. Circumstances also change — an indoor cat can escape, need boarding, or require hospitalization, all of which introduce exposure risk.

Kitten Schedule

Kittens typically receive their first Tricat dose around 6-8 weeks, with a booster around 16 weeks, timed to work around fading maternal antibodies — similar logic to puppy vaccination timing. Adult cats generally move to a booster schedule after the kitten series.

💡 Households with more than one cat, or cats that visit boarding, grooming, or shelter environments, face higher exposure risk. A fully vaccinated cat in a multi-cat home also protects the household as a whole, since disease spreads faster where animals live close together.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can a vaccinated cat still get panleukopenia?
Vaccination greatly reduces risk but no vaccine offers 100% protection — proper vaccination remains the best defense available.

Does my cat need Tricat if she's never left the house?
Yes — the virus can be carried in on shoes, clothing, or visitors, and circumstances like boarding or escape can change exposure risk at any time.

How often does the booster need to be repeated?
Typically annually or on a multi-year cycle depending on the specific vaccine protocol your vet recommends.

Is Tricat the same as FVRCP?
Yes — Tricat is the commonly used name in India for the FVRCP combination vaccine.

cat-not-eating-how-long.title: Cat Not Eating: How Long Is Too Long?
cat-not-eating-how-long.summary: Cats can develop serious complications from not eating faster than dogs. Learn how long is genuinely safe to wait and when it becomes an emergency.
cat-not-eating-how-long.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

Cats are not just small dogs when it comes to appetite loss — a cat that stops eating faces a specific, serious risk that makes this symptom more urgent than it might seem.

Why This Is More Urgent in Cats

Cats that don't eat for an extended period are at risk of a condition called hepatic lipidosis (fatty liver disease), where the body mobilizes fat too quickly and overwhelms the liver — this can happen within just a few days of reduced eating, especially in overweight cats.

The 24-Hour Rule

A cat that hasn't eaten anything in 24 hours should be seen by a vet — this is a shorter window than most owners assume, precisely because of the liver risk described above.

What Might Be Behind It

Dental pain, nausea, stress, respiratory infection affecting smell (which drives appetite in cats), or systemic illness can all cause appetite loss. The cause needs identifying, not just managing symptomatically.

What Not to Do

Don't wait it out hoping your cat will eat when hungry enough — cats don't reliably self-correct this the way some other species might, and the liver risk means time matters.

Frequently Asked Questions

My cat is still drinking water but not eating — is that better?
It's a positive sign for hydration but doesn't eliminate the appetite-loss risk. Still see a vet within 24 hours.

Are overweight cats at higher risk?
Yes, significantly — hepatic lipidosis risk is elevated in overweight cats that stop eating.

Can stress alone explain a cat not eating?
It can cause short-term appetite loss, but the 24-hour rule still applies regardless of suspected cause.

Should I try tempting foods before calling the vet?
You can offer a favorite food, but don't let that delay a vet visit if 24 hours has passed without genuine eating.

parrot-beak-nail-problems.title: Parrot Beak and Nail Problems: When Professional Care Is Needed
parrot-beak-nail-problems.summary: Overgrown beaks or nails can signal underlying health issues in parrots. Learn when trimming needs professional care.
parrot-beak-nail-problems.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

Beak and nail overgrowth in parrots is sometimes normal wear-and-tear related, but can also be the visible sign of a metabolic or liver issue underneath.

Normal Wear vs Overgrowth

Regular access to appropriate perches and chew toys typically keeps beak and nails naturally worn — overgrowth beyond this can indicate insufficient wear opportunities or an underlying issue.

When Overgrowth Signals Illness

Rapid or unusual beak overgrowth can sometimes be linked to liver disease or other metabolic conditions, not just insufficient wear.

Why Trimming Needs Professional Care

Incorrect trimming risks pain, bleeding, and injury — this isn't a safe home procedure without proper training.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I trim my parrot's nails at home?
This carries injury risk without proper training — professional trimming is safer, especially initially.

Does beak overgrowth always mean illness?
Not always, but persistent or rapid overgrowth should be evaluated to rule out underlying causes.

How often do beaks typically need trimming?
This varies by individual bird and available wear opportunities — ask your avian vet for a personalized schedule.

cat-diarrhea-causes-vet-visit.title: Cat Diarrhea: Common Causes and When to Visit a Vet
cat-diarrhea-causes-vet-visit.summary: Diarrhea in cats ranges from a mild diet-related upset to a sign of serious illness. Learn what's manageable at home and what needs a vet visit.
cat-diarrhea-causes-vet-visit.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

Cat diarrhea gets dismissed more often than it should — cats are good at hiding how unwell they feel, so visible digestive symptoms deserve more weight than they often get.

Common, Milder Causes

Sudden diet changes, mild dietary indiscretion, or stress can cause short-lived diarrhea in an otherwise well cat, often resolving within a day or two.

When It Signals Something More

Diarrhea lasting more than a couple of days, blood in the stool, diarrhea combined with vomiting or appetite loss, or diarrhea in a kitten or senior cat should prompt a veterinary visit rather than continued home management.

Possible Underlying Causes

Parasites, dietary intolerance, infections, inflammatory bowel disease, and thyroid or other systemic conditions can all present with diarrhea as a symptom.

Why Kittens Need Faster Attention

Kittens dehydrate much faster than adult cats, so diarrhea that might be manageable in an adult can become dangerous quickly in a kitten.

Frequently Asked Questions

Should I change my cat's food if they have diarrhea?
Not without veterinary guidance — an abrupt additional diet change can sometimes make things worse. A bland, vet-recommended option is safer.

Is diarrhea with normal appetite less concerning?
Somewhat, but persistence beyond a couple of days still warrants evaluation regardless of appetite.

Can indoor-only cats get parasites?
Yes — indoor cats can still pick up parasites through contaminated surfaces, other pets, or even insects.

What should I bring to the vet visit?
A fresh stool sample if possible, and notes on duration, frequency, and any other changes in behavior or appetite.

how-to-tell-bird-in-pain.title: How to Tell If Your Bird Is in Pain
how-to-tell-bird-in-pain.summary: Birds hide pain exceptionally well as an instinctive survival behavior. Learn the subtle signs that indicate discomfort.
how-to-tell-bird-in-pain.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

Recognizing pain in birds requires watching for subtle deviations from normal behavior, since overt pain signals would make a bird look vulnerable in the wild.

Subtle Pain Signs

Reduced activity, fluffed feathers, reluctance to move, changes in perching posture, and reduced vocalization can all indicate discomfort.

Behavioral Changes

A normally social bird becoming withdrawn, or reduced interest in favorite activities, can be pain-related rather than purely behavioral.

When to Seek Care

Any combination of these subtle signs, especially if new or worsening, warrants a veterinary evaluation.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do birds vocalize when in pain?
Not reliably — reduced, not increased, vocalization is often the more telling sign.

Can changes in perching indicate pain?
Yes, favoring one foot or an unusual posture can indicate discomfort.

Is fluffing always a pain sign?
Not always, but persistent fluffing combined with other changes is worth evaluating.

why-is-my-cat-hiding-suddenly.title: Why Is My Cat Hiding Suddenly?
why-is-my-cat-hiding-suddenly.summary: Cats hide when stressed — but also when sick or in pain. Learn how to tell the difference and when sudden hiding behavior needs a vet visit.
why-is-my-cat-hiding-suddenly.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

Cats are masters of concealment, and hiding is one of their most reliable ways of telling you something is wrong — the challenge is figuring out whether it's emotional or medical.

Situational Hiding

New visitors, loud noises, a new pet in the home, or a change in routine can all cause temporary hiding that resolves once the trigger passes and your cat feels secure again.

Medical Hiding

Pain, nausea, and illness are common medical reasons cats withdraw and hide — this is an instinctive behavior rooted in not appearing vulnerable when unwell.

How to Tell the Difference

Situational hiding usually resolves within a day or so and the cat returns to normal behavior. Hiding that persists, or is combined with reduced appetite, changes in litter box habits, or reduced grooming, points toward a medical cause.

When to Act

Persistent hiding beyond a day or two, especially with any other symptom change, warrants a veterinary visit — don't assume it's "just personality" without ruling out pain or illness first.

Frequently Asked Questions

My cat always hides when guests come over — is that normal?
Yes, this is common situational behavior and usually resolves once guests leave.

Can hiding alone (with no other symptoms) still mean illness?
It can, especially if it's a new pattern for your specific cat — cats hide pain very effectively, so a behavior change alone is worth noting.

Does age affect how cats respond to stress?
Yes — older cats and cats with chronic conditions may hide more readily when unwell, making sudden changes more significant to track.

Should I try to coax my cat out of hiding?
Gently, without force — but if it's persistent, focus on getting a veterinary evaluation rather than just managing the behavior.

blood-in-cat-urine-blockage.title: Blood in Cat Urine: Causes, Urinary Blockage, and Emergency Care
blood-in-cat-urine-blockage.summary: Blood in a cat's urine can range from a treatable infection to a life-threatening blockage — especially in male cats. Learn the warning signs.
blood-in-cat-urine-blockage.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

Blood in your cat's urine is never something to watch and wait on — the range of causes includes some of the most urgent conditions in feline medicine.

Possible Causes

Urinary tract infection, bladder inflammation (feline idiopathic cystitis), bladder stones, and urinary blockage can all cause blood in the urine, ranging from uncomfortable to immediately life-threatening.

The Blockage Risk — Especially in Male Cats

Male cats have a narrower urethra and are at higher risk of complete urinary blockage, where blood-tinged urine progresses to no urine output at all. This is one of the true feline emergencies — untreated, it can be fatal within a day or two.

Warning Signs of Blockage

Frequent trips to the litter box with little or no urine produced, straining, crying while attempting to urinate, and licking at the genital area are all signs that need immediate attention, not a wait-and-see approach.

When to Go In Immediately

Any male cat straining with no urine output should be treated as an emergency. Female cats with blood in urine should also be seen promptly, though blockage risk is lower.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is this always a blockage?
No, but it's serious enough that you can't tell the difference from home — a vet visit is needed to determine cause and rule out blockage.

How quickly can blockage become fatal?
It can become life-threatening within 24-48 hours of complete obstruction, which is why it's treated as a top-priority emergency.

Are indoor male cats also at risk?
Yes — this risk isn't related to outdoor access; it's anatomical and can affect any male cat.

What does treatment for blockage involve?
Typically relieving the obstruction (often via catheterization under sedation) and managing resulting complications — this requires immediate in-clinic care.

cat-vomiting-hairballs-or-serious.title: Cat Vomiting Frequently: Normal Hairballs or a Serious Problem?
cat-vomiting-hairballs-or-serious.summary: Occasional hairballs are normal in cats — frequent vomiting is not. Learn to tell the difference and when it signals something more serious.
cat-vomiting-hairballs-or-serious.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

"Cats vomit sometimes, that's normal" is true and also the exact belief that lets real problems go unnoticed for too long.

What's Actually Normal

An occasional hairball, especially in longer-haired cats, brought up once every week or two in an otherwise healthy, active cat is generally not concerning.

What's Not Normal

Vomiting more than once or twice a week, vomiting food (not just hair), weight loss alongside vomiting, or vomiting combined with lethargy or appetite changes all point toward something beyond routine hairballs.

Possible Underlying Causes

Chronic vomiting in cats can stem from dietary intolerance, inflammatory bowel disease, hyperthyroidism, kidney disease, or other chronic conditions — "just hairballs" is a diagnosis of exclusion, not a default assumption.

When to See a Vet

Frequency is the key signal — if you're seeing vomiting weekly or more, or if anything else has changed (appetite, weight, energy), it's time for an actual workup rather than continued at-home monitoring.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does hairball paste prevent all vomiting-related issues?
It can help with hair passage but won't address an underlying medical cause if one exists — don't rely on it if vomiting is frequent.

Is vomiting after eating too fast a concern?
Occasional regurgitation right after fast eating is usually mechanical, not medical — try smaller, slower-paced meals and monitor.

Can chronic vomiting be linked to diet?
Yes — food intolerance or sensitivity is a real and treatable cause worth investigating with your vet.

What tests help find the cause of chronic vomiting?
Bloodwork, and sometimes imaging or further gastrointestinal workup, depending on findings and history.

dog-emergency-vet-signs.title: What Are the Signs That Your Dog Needs an Emergency Vet?
dog-emergency-vet-signs.summary: How to tell the difference between a wait-and-watch symptom and a true emergency in dogs — a clear checklist for pet owners.
dog-emergency-vet-signs.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

Not every symptom needs an emergency visit, and not every “he seems fine” is actually fine. The hardest part of pet ownership is telling the two apart in the moment. Here's a clear-eyed checklist.

💡 Treat these as immediate emergencies: difficulty breathing, collapse or inability to stand, a bloated or painful abdomen (especially in deep-chested breeds), repeated vomiting or seizures, suspected poisoning, severe bleeding, or an inability to urinate. None of these should wait for a “morning appointment.”

Watch Closely, Call If It Continues

A single episode of vomiting in an otherwise bright, active dog, mild limping without swelling, or one instance of loose stool can often be monitored for a few hours — but persistence, worsening, or a combination of symptoms changes that calculus fast.

The Combination Rule

A single mild symptom is usually less urgent than the same symptom appearing alongside others — lethargy plus vomiting plus reduced appetite together is a stronger signal than any one of those alone.

When in Doubt

Call the clinic and describe what you're seeing. A quick phone conversation costs nothing and can tell you in two minutes whether this is a home-monitoring situation or a “come in now” one.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is heavy panting always an emergency?
Not always — panting from heat or exertion is normal, but panting combined with distress, blue-tinged gums, or an inability to settle is not.

My dog seems fine but ate something he shouldn't have — do I wait for symptoms?
No — call your vet immediately. Waiting for symptoms means treatment starts later, which matters for many toxins.

What's a bloated abdomen a sign of?
It can indicate gastric dilatation-volvulus (bloat), a life-threatening emergency especially in large, deep-chested breeds — this needs immediate veterinary attention, not observation.

Should I call ahead before coming in for an emergency?
Yes, if possible — calling Shivraj Pet Clinic & Lab ahead lets the team prepare, which can save critical time.

bird-first-aid-before-avian-vet.title: Bird First Aid: What to Do Before Reaching an Avian Vet
bird-first-aid-before-avian-vet.summary: Basic first-aid steps for common bird emergencies before you can get to an avian vet — bleeding, injury, and shock.
bird-first-aid-before-avian-vet.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

In a bird emergency, the first few minutes of appropriate first aid can meaningfully support your bird until you reach professional care.

For Bleeding

Gentle pressure with a clean cloth on the affected area, and keeping the bird calm and warm, can help manage minor bleeding en route to the vet.

For Suspected Injury or Shock

Keep the bird in a warm, quiet, dark, enclosed space (like a covered carrier) to reduce stress and minimize movement during transport.

What Not to Do

Avoid excessive handling, don't attempt to give food or water to a bird that's unresponsive, and don't apply human medications.

Frequently Asked Questions

Should I try to stop bleeding with home remedies?

Why does keeping the bird warm and dark matter?
It reduces stress, which matters significantly for a bird's condition during an emergency.

why-is-my-cat-losing-weight.title: Why Is My Cat Losing Weight?
why-is-my-cat-losing-weight.summary: Unexplained weight loss in cats — even with normal appetite — often points to an underlying condition. Learn the common causes and when to test.
why-is-my-cat-losing-weight.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

Weight loss in cats is often gradual enough that owners don't notice until it's significant — which is exactly why it's worth tracking actively, not just visually.

Why It's Easy to Miss

A cat's coat can hide weight loss for a while, and gradual change is harder to notice day to day than a sudden shift. Regular weighing, not just visual assessment, catches this earlier.

Common Causes

Hyperthyroidism, diabetes, kidney disease, dental disease affecting eating, intestinal parasites, and inflammatory bowel disease are all common causes of weight loss in cats — several are more common in middle-aged and senior cats.

The Confusing Case of Increased Appetite Plus Weight Loss

Hyperthyroidism specifically can cause a cat to eat more than usual while still losing weight — a combination that seems paradoxical to owners but is a classic textbook presentation of the condition.

What Diagnosis Involves

Bloodwork (including thyroid levels), a physical exam, and sometimes further imaging or fecal testing are the standard starting points for identifying the cause.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is weight loss more concerning in senior cats?
Yes — several common causes are more prevalent in senior cats, making evaluation especially important in this age group.

Should I weigh my cat regularly at home?
It's a useful habit — a kitchen scale for carriers or a baby scale can help track trends between vet visits.

Can dental pain alone cause significant weight loss?
Yes, if it's severe enough to reduce how much or how comfortably your cat eats.

Is hyperthyroidism treatable?
Yes, several management and treatment options exist — your vet can discuss what's appropriate based on diagnosis.

cat-breathing-problems-respiratory-distr.title: Cat Breathing Problems: Signs of Respiratory Distress
cat-breathing-problems-respiratory-distr.summary: Cats hide breathing difficulty exceptionally well. Learn the subtle and obvious signs of respiratory distress and why it's always an emergency.
cat-breathing-problems-respiratory-distr.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

By the time a cat's breathing trouble is obvious to an owner, the underlying problem is often already significant — cats compensate for respiratory distress remarkably well until they can't.

Subtle Early Signs

Breathing with the mouth slightly open (unusual for cats at rest), a faster than normal breathing rate, or reluctance to move and play can be early, easy-to-miss signs.

Obvious Emergency Signs

Open-mouth breathing, blue-tinged gums or tongue, exaggerated abdominal movement with breathing, or a hunched posture with elbows out are all signs of significant respiratory distress and need immediate veterinary attention.

Possible Causes

Asthma, heart disease, fluid in the chest, infections, and, in emergencies, trauma or foreign body obstruction can all cause respiratory distress in cats.

Why This Is Always Treated as Urgent

Cats mask respiratory distress until they're in genuine crisis, so any visible breathing difficulty — even if it seems mild — should be treated as an emergency, not monitored at home.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is occasional fast breathing after play normal?
Yes, brief elevated breathing after activity is normal and should settle within minutes once your cat rests.

Can stress cause breathing changes in cats?
Mild, brief changes can occur, but persistent or labored breathing should never be attributed to stress alone without veterinary evaluation.

Is asthma common in cats?
It's a recognized condition in cats and can cause episodes of respiratory distress requiring management.

Should I try to keep my cat calm on the way to the vet?
Yes — minimize handling and stress during transport, as anxiety can worsen breathing difficulty.

puppy-deworming-schedule-india.title: Puppy Deworming Schedule in India: First Dose to Regular Prevention
puppy-deworming-schedule-india.summary: A clear puppy deworming schedule for Indian pet owners — when to start, how often to repeat, and why the timing matters.
puppy-deworming-schedule-india.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

Like kittens, puppies are commonly born with or quickly exposed to intestinal parasites, making a structured deworming schedule an early, essential part of care.

Starting the Schedule

Deworming typically begins around 2-3 weeks of age, repeating every 2-3 weeks through the early puppy months before transitioning to a regular adult schedule.

Why Repeated Doses Matter

A single dose doesn't address parasites at every life stage present in a growing puppy's system — the repeated schedule is designed around this.

Signs of a Parasite Burden

A pot-bellied appearance, poor growth, visible worms in stool, and diarrhea can indicate parasites needing attention.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is deworming safe for very young puppies?
Yes, with age-appropriate products and veterinary guidance.

Can puppies get parasites from their mother?
Yes, this is a common transmission route, which is why early deworming matters.

When does deworming frequency decrease?
Typically after the puppy series completes, transitioning to a regular adult schedule.

bird-breathing-problem.title: Bird Breathing Problems — Warning Signs & When to Rush to the Vet in Pune
bird-breathing-problem.summary: Tail-bobbing, open-beak breathing, or a fluffed-up posture in a pet bird can signal a respiratory emergency. Learn the warning signs from Shivraj Pet Clinic, Wakad & Pimple Saudagar, Pune.
bird-breathing-problem.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Medicine), Head Veterinarian at Shivraj Pet Clinic & Exotic Animal Centre.

Birds are prey animals by instinct, which means they hide illness extremely well — by the time breathing difficulty is visible, the underlying problem is often already advanced. At Shivraj Pet Clinic & Exotic Animal Centre, Wakad & Pimple Saudagar, Pune, we treat respiratory distress in pet birds as an emergency.

Quick Facts

Species affectedBudgies, cockatiels, conures, and other pet birds
SeverityCan be life-threatening; birds decline quickly once visibly distressed
Common causesRespiratory infection, air sac issues, inhaled irritants, egg-related complications
Emergency signsTail-bobbing with each breath, open-beak breathing, audible clicking or wheezing
PreventionGood ventilation, avoiding aerosols/fumes near birds, routine wellness checks

Why Breathing Problems in Birds Are Always Urgent

A bird's respiratory system is different from a mammal's — it's highly efficient at extracting oxygen, but that also means a bird already breathing visibly hard has very little reserve left. What looks like a "sudden" breathing problem is frequently the final, visible stage of something that's been developing quietly for days.

Common Causes

  • Respiratory infections — bacterial, fungal, or viral, often affecting the airway or air sacs
  • Inhaled irritants — non-stick cookware fumes, aerosols, scented candles, and smoke are genuinely dangerous to birds
  • Air sac or lung disease — including chronic conditions that worsen gradually
  • Egg-related complications — such as egg binding in female birds, which can restrict normal breathing
  • Obesity or fatty liver disease — can reduce normal breathing capacity over time

Warning Signs to Watch For

  • Tail bobbing up and down with each breath
  • Open-beak breathing, especially at rest
  • Audible clicking, wheezing, or a change in voice/chirp
  • Fluffed-up feathers with lethargy
  • Sitting low on the perch or at the bottom of the cage
  • Discharge from the nostrils (nares) or around the eyes
⚠️ Any bird showing tail-bobbing, open-beak breathing, or audible respiratory sounds needs to be seen immediately. Birds can decline within hours once breathing distress is visibly obvious — this is not a "wait and watch" situation.

What Happens at the Clinic

  • Low-stress handling and examination — birds can decompensate from stress alone, so handling is kept brief and calm
  • Oxygen support — provided immediately where needed, often before a full workup
  • Diagnostic imaging — X-rays to assess the lungs, air sacs, and check for egg-related causes
  • Laboratory testing — to identify infection and guide antibiotic or antifungal treatment
  • Environmental correction — advice on removing any household irritant contributing to the problem

Prevention

  • Never use non-stick cookware, aerosol sprays, scented candles, or air fresheners in rooms where birds are kept — fumes that are mild for humans can be fatal to birds
  • Ensure good ventilation and avoid smoking near your bird
  • Watch daily for subtle changes in activity, voice, or posture, since birds mask illness until it's advanced
  • Book routine wellness checks even when your bird seems healthy
  • Maintain a healthy weight and balanced diet to reduce the risk of fatty liver and related breathing issues

Frequently Asked Questions

My bird's tail moves a little when it breathes — is that normal?
A very slight movement can be normal, but pronounced, rhythmic bobbing with every breath is a warning sign and should be checked promptly.

Could a scented candle really affect my bird's breathing?
Yes — birds have an extremely sensitive respiratory system, and fumes from non-stick cookware, aerosols, and some scented products can cause acute, sometimes fatal, respiratory distress.

Is breathing difficulty always respiratory, or could it be something else?
Not always — conditions like egg binding or fatty liver disease can also restrict normal breathing, which is why a full exam matters rather than assuming it's a lung infection.

How is a bird's breathing problem diagnosed?
Through a calm physical exam, often combined with X-rays and lab testing once the bird is stable enough for handling.

My bird seems fine most of the day but breathes harder after activity — should I be concerned?
Yes, reduced exercise tolerance is worth a check — it can be an early sign before breathing problems appear at rest.

Do you treat budgies and cockatiels as well as larger birds?
Yes, we see a wide range of pet bird species at our Exotic Animal Centre.

guinea-pig-dental-problem.title: Guinea Pig Dental Problems — Overgrown Teeth Symptoms & Treatment in Pune
guinea-pig-dental-problem.summary: Drooling, weight loss, or dropping food while eating can signal overgrown teeth in a guinea pig. Learn the warning signs from Shivraj Pet Clinic, Wakad & Pimple Saudagar, Pune.
guinea-pig-dental-problem.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Medicine), Head Veterinarian at Shivraj Pet Clinic & Exotic Animal Centre.

Guinea pig teeth grow continuously throughout life — which means dental problems are one of the most common, and most under-recognised, health issues we see at Shivraj Pet Clinic & Exotic Animal Centre, Wakad & Pimple Saudagar, Pune.

Quick Facts

Species affectedDomestic pet guinea pigs, all ages
SeveritySerious if untreated — leads to weight loss and secondary infection
Common causesLow-fibre diet, genetics, insufficient chewing material
Emergency signsDrooling, complete refusal to eat, visible facial swelling
PreventionUnlimited hay, regular dental checks, appropriate chew items

Why Dental Problems Are So Common in Guinea Pigs

Unlike humans, a guinea pig's molars and incisors never stop growing. Normally, a high-fibre diet wears them down evenly through constant chewing. When diet lacks enough coarse fibre, or teeth grow unevenly, sharp points and overgrowth can develop — often on the back molars, where it's not visible without a proper oral exam.

Common Causes

  • Low-fibre diet — too many pellets and treats, not enough hay
  • Genetic predisposition — some guinea pigs are simply more prone to malocclusion
  • Insufficient wear — not enough coarse material to chew regularly
  • Untreated minor misalignment — small issues that worsen gradually if not corrected

Warning Signs to Watch For

  • Drooling or a consistently wet chin
  • Dropping food while attempting to eat, or chewing on one side only
  • Weight loss despite food being available
  • Reduced or no interest in hard foods or hay
  • Facial swelling near the jawline
  • Reduced grooming, leading to a scruffy coat
⚠️ A guinea pig that stops eating for more than a few hours needs urgent attention — like rabbits, guinea pigs can decline quickly once food intake drops, regardless of the underlying cause.

What Happens at the Clinic

  • Oral examination — back molars often require sedation to examine properly, since they're not visible on a casual look
  • Dental correction — filing or trimming overgrown or sharp points under appropriate sedation
  • Pain management — dental pain is often significant and addressed alongside the correction itself
  • Nutritional support — syringe feeding where needed while the mouth heals
  • Follow-up monitoring — since guinea pig teeth keep growing, some cases need periodic rechecks

Prevention

  • Provide unlimited access to good-quality grass hay as the majority of the diet
  • Limit pellets and treats to the recommended amount rather than free-feeding them
  • Offer safe chew items to encourage natural wear
  • Book a dental check if you notice any change in eating pattern, even a subtle one
  • Weigh your guinea pig regularly — gradual weight loss is often the earliest sign of a developing problem

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I check my guinea pig's back teeth myself at home?
Not reliably — the molars sit far back and require proper equipment and often sedation to examine safely and thoroughly.

Will my guinea pig need repeat dental treatments?
Some guinea pigs, especially those with a genetic predisposition to malocclusion, need periodic dental rechecks throughout life.

My guinea pig is still eating pellets but avoiding hay — is that a concern?
Yes — preferring soft food over hay is a common early sign of dental discomfort and is worth checking before it progresses.

Is dental treatment safe for guinea pigs, given they need sedation?
Yes, with appropriate pre-anaesthetic assessment, sedation for dental work is a routine and safe procedure for guinea pigs.

How much hay does my guinea pig actually need?
As a general guide, hay should make up the majority of daily intake, roughly an amount equal to your guinea pig's own body size, available at all times.
