rabbit-not-eating.title: Rabbit Not Eating? Causes, Emergency Signs & Treatment in Pune
rabbit-not-eating.summary: A rabbit that stops eating for even a few hours can be a genuine emergency, not something to wait out. Learn why, and what to do, from Shivraj Pet Clinic, Wakad & Pimple Saudagar, Pune.
rabbit-not-eating.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Medicine), Head Veterinarian at Shivraj Pet Clinic & Exotic Animal Centre.

Unlike dogs or cats, a rabbit that skips even one or two meals is not "just being fussy" — it's one of the most time-sensitive warning signs in rabbit medicine. At Shivraj Pet Clinic & Exotic Animal Centre, Wakad & Pimple Saudagar, Pune, we treat rabbit anorexia as an emergency until proven otherwise.

Quick Facts

Species affectedDomestic pet rabbits, all breeds and ages
SeverityCan be life-threatening within 24-48 hours if untreated
Common causesGI stasis, dental disease, pain, stress, dietary changes
Emergency signsNo food or droppings for 12+ hours, hunched posture, teeth grinding
PreventionHigh-fibre hay-based diet, regular dental checks, low-stress environment

Why Rabbits Not Eating Is a Genuine Emergency

Rabbits have a digestive system that depends on constant movement. When food intake stops, gut motility can slow or halt entirely — a condition called GI stasis. Gas builds up, the gut environment shifts, and without prompt treatment this can become life-threatening within a day or two, not weeks.

This is different from a dog or cat skipping a meal out of stress or a mild stomach upset. In rabbits, the loss of appetite is very often a symptom of an underlying problem, not the problem itself — most commonly dental pain, an obstruction, or a painful condition elsewhere in the body.

Common Causes

  • Dental disease — overgrown or misaligned molars causing pain while chewing
  • GI stasis — slowed or stopped gut motility, often secondary to low-fibre diet, stress, or pain
  • Obstruction — a blockage from ingested fur or foreign material
  • Pain from another source — such as a urinary issue, arthritis, or an abscess
  • Stress — a change in environment, a new cage-mate, or a frightening event

Warning Signs to Watch For

  • No food eaten for several hours, or dramatically reduced interest in favourite foods
  • Fewer or no droppings being produced
  • Hunched, tense posture with reluctance to move
  • Teeth grinding (a common sign of pain in rabbits)
  • A bloated or firm abdomen
  • Lethargy or hiding more than usual
⚠️ If your rabbit hasn't eaten or produced droppings in 12 hours or more, treat it as an emergency and contact a veterinarian immediately. Do not wait to "see if it improves" — early intervention makes a major difference in outcome.

What Happens at the Clinic

  • Physical examination — including a full dental check, since molar problems are a leading cause
  • Pain assessment and management — rabbits mask pain well, so this is central to treatment
  • Fluid therapy — to rehydrate and help restart gut motility
  • Gut-motility medication — where appropriate, once obstruction has been ruled out
  • Imaging — X-rays to check for obstruction or excessive gas build-up when indicated

Prevention

  • Feed a diet that's primarily good-quality grass hay, supplemented with fresh leafy greens
  • Keep fresh water available at all times
  • Book regular dental checks, since overgrown molars often cause no obvious external signs until eating stops
  • Minimise sudden changes to diet, housing, or companions where possible
  • Monitor daily food intake and droppings — catching a change early is the biggest factor in a good outcome

Frequently Asked Questions

My rabbit ate a little this morning but has stopped since — is that still an emergency?
Yes. A significant drop in intake, even if not complete refusal, warrants a same-day check, especially if droppings have also reduced.

Can I just syringe-feed my rabbit at home until it improves?
Supportive feeding can help once a vet has assessed the cause, but doing it alone without knowing why your rabbit stopped eating can delay treatment of the underlying problem.

Is GI stasis the same as a hairball blockage?
Not always — stasis is a slowdown of gut movement that can happen with or without a physical blockage. Only an exam (and sometimes imaging) can tell the difference.

How quickly can rabbits decline once they stop eating?
Deterioration can happen within 24-48 hours, which is why same-day veterinary attention matters so much with this species.

Do you see rabbit dental problems often?
Yes — dental disease is one of the most common underlying causes of appetite loss we diagnose in pet rabbits.

What should I bring to the appointment?
Note roughly when your rabbit last ate and last produced droppings, and bring your rabbit in its normal carrier to minimise added stress.

turtle-shell-rot.title: Turtle Shell Rot — Causes, Symptoms & Treatment in Pune
turtle-shell-rot.summary: Soft patches, discoloration, or a foul smell from your turtle's shell can signal shell rot — a treatable but serious infection. Learn the signs from Shivraj Pet Clinic, Wakad & Pimple Saudagar, Pune.
turtle-shell-rot.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Medicine), Head Veterinarian at Shivraj Pet Clinic & Exotic Animal Centre.

"Shell rot" is one of the most common reasons pet turtles are brought to Shivraj Pet Clinic & Exotic Animal Centre, Wakad & Pimple Saudagar, Pune — and one of the most preventable, once the underlying husbandry issue is corrected.

Quick Facts

Species affectedAquatic and semi-aquatic pet turtles
SeveritySerious if untreated — can spread to bone in advanced cases
Common causesPoor water quality, inadequate basking/UVB, shell injury, overcrowding
Emergency signsSoft or pitted shell areas, foul odour, discharge, visible discoloration
PreventionClean water, proper filtration, adequate dry basking time, UVB lighting

What Shell Rot Actually Is

Shell rot is a bacterial or fungal infection of the shell — it's not a single disease but a description of what happens when the shell's protective outer layer breaks down, usually because of prolonged exposure to dirty water or insufficient time basking dry. Once the surface is compromised, bacteria or fungi can take hold in the underlying tissue.

Common Causes

  • Poor water quality — infrequent water changes or inadequate filtration
  • Insufficient basking — turtles need real dry-out time under a proper basking light to keep the shell healthy
  • Shell injury — a crack, scrape, or old wound that becomes infected
  • Overcrowding — multiple turtles in too small a space increases stress and bacterial load
  • Poor UVB exposure — contributes to weaker shell condition overall

Warning Signs to Watch For

  • Soft, pitted, or flaking patches on the shell
  • Discoloration — white, yellow, red, or dark patches that weren't there before
  • A foul smell coming from the shell
  • Visible discharge or a chalky residue over affected areas
  • Reduced appetite or activity in more advanced cases
⚠️ Don't attempt to treat visible shell rot at home with over-the-counter products before a veterinary exam. Untreated or incorrectly treated shell rot can progress to the bone underneath, which is far harder — and more expensive — to treat.

What Happens at the Clinic

  • Examination of the affected area — to assess how deep the infection has progressed
  • Debridement — careful cleaning of affected shell tissue where needed
  • Topical or systemic medication — antibacterial or antifungal treatment based on what's found
  • Habitat review — water quality, filtration, and basking setup are checked, since treatment fails if the underlying cause isn't fixed
  • Follow-up monitoring — shell healing is slow, so progress is tracked over several visits

Prevention

  • Change water regularly and use adequate filtration for your turtle's tank size
  • Provide a proper dry basking area with appropriate heat and UVB lighting
  • Avoid overcrowding — give each turtle enough space
  • Inspect the shell during regular handling so early changes are caught quickly
  • Address any shell injury promptly rather than waiting to see if it heals on its own

Frequently Asked Questions

Is shell rot contagious to other turtles?
The underlying bacteria or fungi can potentially spread in shared, poor-quality water, so it's sensible to review the whole tank setup, not just the affected turtle.

Can shell rot heal on its own?
Mild cases occasionally improve once water quality is corrected, but by the time it's visible, veterinary assessment is strongly recommended to prevent progression.

Will the shell look completely normal again after treatment?
Often shell texture and color improve significantly, though severe cases can leave some permanent surface changes even after the infection clears.

How long does treatment take?
This varies with severity — mild cases may resolve in a few weeks, while advanced cases can take months of consistent treatment and habitat correction.

Is shell rot the same as the "floating sideways" problem I've read about?
No — floating issues are usually related to buoyancy or respiratory problems, a separate concern from shell rot, though both often stem from husbandry issues.

Do land tortoises get shell rot too?
It's far less common in tortoises since they aren't in water constantly, but shell infections can still occur from injury or persistent damp housing.

cat-fever-symptoms.title: Cat Fever Symptoms and When to See a Veterinarian
cat-fever-symptoms.summary: Recognizing fever in cats is harder than in dogs since cats hide illness so well. Learn the real signs and when a fever needs veterinary attention.
cat-fever-symptoms.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

Cats hide fever even more effectively than dogs do, which means owners often only notice once the cat is clearly unwell — knowing the subtler signs helps catch it earlier.

Signs of Fever in Cats

Lethargy, reduced interest in food, hiding more than usual, warm ears, and a generally "off" demeanor are common signs. Cats often show fewer obvious behavioral changes than dogs, making close observation important.

Confirming It Accurately

A proper rectal temperature reading with a pet-appropriate thermometer is the only reliable way to confirm fever — visual or touch-based guessing isn't accurate enough in cats.

Common Causes

Infections, inflammation, abscesses (common after fights or bites), and less commonly immune-mediated conditions can all cause fever in cats.

When to See a Vet

Fever lasting more than a day, a high reading, or fever combined with lethargy, appetite loss, or hiding behavior should prompt a veterinary visit. Never give human fever medication to a cat — cats are especially sensitive to several common human drugs, including paracetamol, which can be fatal.

Frequently Asked Questions

Are cats more sensitive to human medications than dogs?
Yes, significantly — several common human drugs that are risky for dogs are outright dangerous or fatal for cats. Never medicate a cat without veterinary guidance.

Can an abscess from a fight cause fever?
Yes, this is a common cause, especially in cats with outdoor access — check for wounds if fever appears after a suspected fight.

Is a warm nose a reliable sign in cats too?
No, same as in dogs — nose temperature isn't a reliable fever indicator on its own.

How is fever treated in cats?
Treatment addresses the underlying cause; your vet will determine appropriate management based on diagnosis rather than treating the fever symptom alone.

dog-not-eating-drinking.title: Dog Not Eating or Drinking: When Should You Worry?
dog-not-eating-drinking.summary: A dog that skips one meal isn't always cause for alarm — but a dog that won't eat or drink for over 24 hours is. Here's how to tell the difference.
dog-not-eating-drinking.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

Appetite is one of the clearest windows into your dog's health — which is exactly why a sudden change in eating or drinking deserves real attention, not just a shrug.

One Skipped Meal vs. a Pattern

A dog that skips one meal but remains playful, alert, and drinking normally is usually fine — stress, a minor stomach upset, or a hot day can all cause this. A dog that refuses food across multiple meals, or stops drinking water entirely, is a different situation.

💡 Dogs can go longer without food than without water. A dog that won't drink for 24 hours is at real risk of dehydration, which compounds whatever the underlying problem is. Not drinking is generally a stronger signal to act on than not eating alone.

What Might Be Behind It

Causes range from mild (dental pain, a recent vaccination, travel stress) to serious (infection, organ disease, gastrointestinal obstruction). Because the range is so wide, a physical exam — and sometimes bloodwork — is often the fastest way to actually know what's happening rather than guessing.

When to Bring Your Dog In

More than 24 hours without eating, any period without drinking water, or reduced appetite alongside vomiting, lethargy, or weight loss all warrant a veterinary visit rather than continued home monitoring.

Frequently Asked Questions

My puppy isn't eating — is that more urgent than in an adult dog?
Yes. Puppies have smaller reserves and can become weak or hypoglycemic faster than adult dogs, so the window for “wait and see” is much shorter.

Can stress alone cause a dog to stop eating?
Yes — travel, a new home, loud noises, or a change in routine can all temporarily suppress appetite, but this should resolve within a day or so.

Should I try to force-feed my dog?
No — force-feeding a dog that's nauseous or unwell can cause more harm than good. Get a veterinary opinion first.

Does not drinking always mean dehydration is imminent?
Not immediately, but the risk builds quickly, especially in small dogs, puppies, and hot weather — don't wait a full day to act.

dog-deworming-frequency.title: How Often Should Dogs Be Dewormed?
dog-deworming-frequency.summary: Deworming frequency for adult dogs depends on lifestyle and risk factors. Here's a general guide for Indian pet owners.
dog-deworming-frequency.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

Once past the puppy schedule, deworming frequency for adult dogs isn't one-size-fits-all — lifestyle and exposure risk play a real role.

General Guidance

Many vets recommend deworming adult dogs every 3-6 months, though this can vary based on your dog's environment and risk exposure.

Higher-Risk Factors

Dogs that frequent parks, have contact with other animals, or live in higher-exposure environments may need more frequent deworming.

Why It's Not Purely Symptom-Based

Parasites aren't always visibly obvious, so scheduled prevention matters more than waiting for signs to appear.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do indoor dogs need less frequent deworming?
Generally somewhat, but exposure through walks and other pets still applies — ask your vet for a personalized schedule.

Can deworming products vary in what they cover?
Yes, different products target different parasite types — your vet can advise the right one.

Is fecal testing useful alongside scheduled deworming?

feline-panleukopenia-vs-cat-flu.title: Feline Panleukopenia vs Cat Flu: How to Tell the Difference
feline-panleukopenia-vs-cat-flu.summary: Panleukopenia and cat flu share some symptoms but differ significantly in severity and treatment. Learn how vets tell them apart.
feline-panleukopenia-vs-cat-flu.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

Feline panleukopenia and "cat flu" (upper respiratory infection) can look similar at first glance in a sick cat, but they're different diseases with different severity levels — which is why an accurate diagnosis, not a guess based on symptoms alone, matters. For a full breakdown of panleukopenia specifically, see our detailed article on Feline Panleukopenia.

Feline Panleukopenia — the Basics

Caused by feline parvovirus, panleukopenia primarily attacks the intestinal tract and immune system, causing vomiting, diarrhea, severe lethargy, and dangerously low white blood cell counts. It is one of the more life-threatening infectious diseases in cats, especially kittens.

Cat Flu — the Basics

Usually caused by feline herpesvirus or calicivirus, cat flu primarily affects the upper respiratory tract — sneezing, nasal discharge, eye discharge, and sometimes mouth ulcers. It's generally less severe than panleukopenia, though it can still make cats quite unwell, especially kittens and cats with weaker immune systems.

Key Differences

Panleukopenia is predominantly a gastrointestinal and systemic disease; cat flu is predominantly respiratory. Panleukopenia carries a higher risk of rapid, severe deterioration, particularly in unvaccinated kittens.

Why Testing Matters

Because early symptoms can overlap — lethargy and reduced appetite appear in both — laboratory testing helps distinguish between them accurately rather than relying on symptom pattern alone, which changes how urgently and how the case is managed.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can a cat have both at the same time?
It's possible for a cat to be exposed to multiple pathogens, particularly in higher-risk multi-cat environments, which is another reason testing matters.

Does the Tricat vaccine protect against both?
Yes — Tricat (FVRCP) covers feline panleukopenia as well as key respiratory pathogens involved in cat flu.

Is cat flu ever dangerous?
It can be, particularly in kittens, senior cats, or cats with weakened immune systems — it shouldn't be dismissed as automatically mild.

Which is more contagious?
Both are highly contagious among cats, spreading through direct contact and contaminated environments, which is why isolation of sick cats matters for either.

dog-vomiting-causes.title: Why Is My Dog Vomiting? Common Causes and When It Becomes an Emergency
dog-vomiting-causes.summary: Vomiting in dogs ranges from a mild one-off to a life-threatening emergency. Here's how to tell which one you're dealing with.
dog-vomiting-causes.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

Vomiting is one of the most common reasons dogs see a vet — and one of the hardest symptoms to judge from the outside, because the same symptom can mean almost nothing or something serious. If your dog's vomiting is paired with diarrhea, our dedicated article on gastroenteritis in dogs covers that combination in more depth.

Common, Lower-Concern Causes

Eating too fast, a sudden diet change, mild dietary indiscretion (raiding the bin), or motion sickness during travel can all cause a single vomiting episode in an otherwise normal, active dog.

When It's More Serious

Repeated vomiting, vomit containing blood, vomiting alongside lethargy or abdominal pain, or vomiting in a dog that's also not eating or drinking all point toward something that needs veterinary evaluation — ranging from infection to pancreatitis to a foreign body obstruction.

💡 Dogs, especially young ones, swallow objects they shouldn't — toys, socks, bones, string. Persistent vomiting, refusal to eat, and abdominal discomfort together can signal an obstruction, which is a surgical emergency, not a wait-it-out situation.

What Your Vet Will Want to Know

How many times, over what timeframe, what the vomit looks like (clear, bile-yellow, food, blood), whether your dog has access to anything they shouldn't have eaten, and what else is going on — appetite, energy, stool. Having these details ready speeds up the visit.

Frequently Asked Questions

My dog vomited once and is acting completely normal — should I still worry?
Usually not, but skip the next meal and offer small amounts of water; call your vet if a second episode happens or your dog seems off.

What does it mean if there's blood in the vomit?
This should always prompt a veterinary visit — it can indicate anything from irritation to a more serious internal issue.

Can diet changes cause vomiting?
Yes — switching foods too abruptly is a common, usually mild, cause. Transition new foods gradually over several days.

How do vets diagnose the cause of vomiting?
Depending on the case, this may involve a physical exam, bloodwork, X-rays, or ultrasound — see our article on advanced pet diagnostics for more detail.

cat-vaccination-schedule-india.title: Cat Vaccination Schedule in India: Kitten Vaccines and Booster Shots
cat-vaccination-schedule-india.summary: A clear kitten and adult cat vaccination schedule for Indian pet owners — core vaccines, timing, and booster intervals explained.
cat-vaccination-schedule-india.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

Cat vaccination follows a similar logic to dog vaccination — timed doses that work around fading maternal immunity — but the specific vaccines and considerations differ.

Kitten Schedule

The core Tricat (FVRCP) vaccine typically starts around 6-8 weeks, with a booster around 16 weeks. Rabies vaccination is generally added into the schedule as well, timed according to your vet's protocol and local regulations.

Adult Booster Schedule

After the kitten series, adult cats typically move to a booster schedule — often annual or multi-year depending on the specific vaccine, following your vet's recommendation based on lifestyle and risk.

Lifestyle Considerations

Outdoor cats, cats in multi-cat households, and cats with shelter or boarding exposure may need additional consideration in their vaccination plan compared to a strictly indoor, single-cat household — though as covered in our indoor-cats article, indoor status alone doesn't eliminate the need for core vaccines.

Building an Individual Plan

A rescued adult cat with unknown vaccine history and a kitten from a known breeder need different starting points. At Shivraj Pet Clinic & Lab, we tailor the schedule to your cat's actual history rather than a one-size-fits-all chart.

Frequently Asked Questions

What if I don't know my adopted cat's vaccine history?
Your vet will typically treat them as unvaccinated and start an appropriate catch-up schedule.

Is rabies vaccination necessary for indoor cats?
It's generally recommended regardless of indoor/outdoor status, partly due to legal requirements and partly because circumstances can change unexpectedly.

How often do adult booster shots repeat?
This depends on the specific vaccine — some are annual, others multi-year — your vet will set the exact schedule.

Can kittens be vaccinated too early?
Yes — vaccinating before maternal antibodies fade can reduce vaccine effectiveness, which is why the timed schedule matters.

What if the shelter gave partial vaccination records?

kitten-deworming-schedule-india.title: Kitten Deworming Schedule in India: When and Why It Matters
kitten-deworming-schedule-india.summary: Kittens are commonly born with or quickly pick up intestinal parasites. Here's the deworming schedule and why timing matters for their development.
kitten-deworming-schedule-india.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

Deworming isn't a one-time task — it's a schedule, and kittens in particular need it started early and repeated on a specific timeline because of how easily they pick up parasites.

Why Kittens Are High-Risk

Kittens can be born with parasites transmitted from the mother, or pick them up quickly through nursing or their environment. Left untreated, parasites can cause poor growth, a pot-bellied appearance, diarrhea, and weakness.

General Schedule Pattern

Deworming for kittens typically starts around 2-3 weeks of age and repeats every 2-3 weeks until around 12 weeks, then transitions to a regular adult schedule. Your vet will set the exact intervals based on your kitten's situation.

Signs of a Parasite Burden

A pot-bellied appearance despite otherwise normal or thin body condition, poor growth, visible worms or segments in stool, diarrhea, and a dull coat can all indicate a parasite burden worth addressing promptly.

Why the Schedule Matters More Than a Single Dose

A single deworming dose doesn't cover parasites at every life stage present in the kitten's system — the repeated schedule is designed to catch parasites as they cycle through, which a one-off treatment misses.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can kittens be dewormed before they show any symptoms?
Yes — deworming is typically done on a preventive schedule regardless of visible symptoms, since parasites are extremely common in kittens.

Is deworming safe for very young kittens?
Yes, when using age-appropriate products and dosing under veterinary guidance.

Can humans catch parasites from kittens?
Some parasites are zoonotic (transmissible to humans), which is another reason to stay on schedule and practice good hygiene, especially with children in the home.

When does a kitten move to adult deworming frequency?
Typically after completing the kitten series around 12 weeks, transitioning to a regular adult schedule your vet will outline.

Until the vaccination series is far enough along, puppies are more vulnerable to certain serious diseases present in contaminated environments.

A Balanced Approach

Many vets recommend controlled, low-risk socialization — private, healthy-known dogs and clean environments — rather than full public dog parks before vaccination is more complete.

Why Socialization Still Matters

The early weeks are a critical socialization window, so avoiding all exposure isn't ideal either — the goal is managed exposure, not zero exposure.

Is it safe to walk a puppy on a leash in public before full vaccination?
Generally lower-risk than dog parks, but ask your vet for specific guidance based on your puppy's schedule.

Can puppy classes happen before vaccination is complete?

dog-diarrhea-causes.title: Dog Diarrhea: Causes, Warning Signs, and When to Visit a Vet
dog-diarrhea-causes.summary: Diarrhea in dogs can be a mild, self-limiting upset or a sign of something more serious. Learn the warning signs that mean it's time to see a vet.
dog-diarrhea-causes.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

Diarrhea is common enough that it's tempting to dismiss — but the difference between a one-day upset and a serious problem often comes down to a few specific warning signs, not just how it looks.

Mild, Self-Limiting Diarrhea

A single episode of soft stool in a dog that's otherwise bright, eating normally, and not showing other symptoms is often caused by a minor dietary indiscretion or stress, and frequently resolves within a day with a bland diet.

💡 Diarrhea lasting more than 24-48 hours, blood in the stool, black or tarry stool, diarrhea combined with vomiting or lethargy, or diarrhea in a puppy or senior dog all warrant veterinary evaluation rather than home management.

Why Puppies and Seniors Are Different

Both groups dehydrate faster and have less physiological reserve than a healthy adult dog. What might be a manageable day-long upset in a healthy adult can become dangerous much faster in a young puppy or an older dog with other health conditions.

What Might Be Behind Persistent Diarrhea

Causes range from dietary indiscretion and parasites to infections, food intolerance, and — in more serious cases — gastroenteritis or systemic illness. Persistent or worsening diarrhea usually needs diagnostic workup, not just a diet change, to identify the actual cause.

Frequently Asked Questions

Should I withhold food if my dog has diarrhea?
A short period of a bland, easily digestible diet is often recommended, but check with your vet rather than fasting for an extended period, especially in small or young dogs.

Is blood in the stool always serious?
It should always be evaluated — it can range from mild irritation to something requiring urgent treatment, and it's not something to diagnose from home.

Can stress cause diarrhea in dogs?
Yes — travel, boarding, or a change in routine are common, usually mild and short-lived triggers.

When does diarrhea count as an emergency versus a routine visit?
Diarrhea alongside vomiting, lethargy, blood, or in a very young or senior dog should be treated with more urgency than a same-day-improving case in an otherwise healthy adult.

cat-health-checkup-frequency.title: How Often Should You Take Your Cat for a Health Checkup?
cat-health-checkup-frequency.summary: Cats hide illness exceptionally well, which makes regular checkups more important than owners often realize. Here's a recommended frequency by life stage.
cat-health-checkup-frequency.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

Cats are the masters of looking fine right up until they're not — which is exactly the argument for scheduled checkups rather than waiting for visible symptoms to prompt a visit.

Young, Healthy Adult Cats

An annual checkup is generally recommended for healthy adult cats — covering a physical exam, weight tracking, and a conversation about vaccination and preventive care status.

Senior Cats

Cats generally considered senior (roughly 7+ years, with "geriatric" starting later) benefit from more frequent checkups — often every six months — since several common feline conditions (kidney disease, hyperthyroidism, dental disease) become more likely with age and progress faster without monitoring.

Why Frequency Increases with Age

Many age-related conditions develop gradually and produce few early symptoms — regular bloodwork and exams catch changes before they become obvious problems, which matters more as risk increases.

Between Scheduled Visits

Any new symptom — appetite change, weight change, litter box habit change, behavior change — warrants an unscheduled visit regardless of when the last checkup was.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is an annual checkup enough for a healthy 3-year-old cat?
Generally yes, assuming no ongoing health concerns — your vet can confirm what's appropriate for your specific cat.

What age is considered senior for cats?
Roughly 7 years and older is commonly used as the starting point for increased monitoring, though this can vary.

Does checkup frequency change for cats with chronic conditions?
Yes — cats managing an ongoing condition often need more frequent monitoring than the general age-based guideline.

What does a standard checkup include?
Typically a physical exam, weight and body condition assessment, and a discussion of vaccination and preventive care status; bloodwork is often added for senior cats or as clinically indicated.

pet-missed-vaccine-booster.summary: Missing a scheduled booster doesn't always mean starting over, but timing matters. Here's what to actually do.

A significant delay may reduce protection or require a modified catch-up approach — contact your vet promptly rather than waiting further.

Call your vet as soon as you realize a booster was missed, rather than waiting for the next scheduled visit, to get specific guidance for your pet's situation.

How late is too late for a booster?
This varies by vaccine — your vet can advise based on the specific one missed and the delay length.

Does a missed booster mean no protection at all?

Should I be worried if my adult dog missed one annual booster?
Contact your vet for guidance rather than assuming either full protection or the need to restart.

rabies-dogs-cats-prevention.summary: Rabies remains a serious concern in India. Learn the symptoms, why vaccination is essential, and prevention steps for pet owners.
rabies-dogs-cats-prevention.content:

Rabies is one of the most serious, and most preventable, diseases affecting dogs and cats — vaccination remains the single most effective protection available.

Why Vaccination Is Essential

Rabies is fatal once symptoms appear, in both animals and humans, which makes prevention through vaccination the only truly effective strategy.

Recognizing Possible Symptoms

Behavioral changes, aggression or unusual timidity, excessive drooling, and difficulty swallowing can be signs — any suspected case needs immediate professional attention, not home assessment.

Prevention Beyond Vaccination

Avoiding contact between your pet and unknown or stray animals, and keeping vaccination current, are important additional layers of protection.

Frequently Asked Questions

How often does the rabies vaccine need boosting?
This depends on the specific vaccine and local regulations — ask your vet for the current schedule.

What should I do if my pet is bitten by an unknown animal?
Seek veterinary attention immediately, regardless of your pet's vaccination status.

Is rabies vaccination legally required?
It's strongly recommended and often required under local regulations — check current requirements with your vet.

bad-breath-dogs-dental-disease-sign.summary: Not all bad breath is normal — persistent odor is often an early sign of dental disease in dogs. Learn what to watch for.
bad-breath-dogs-dental-disease-sign.content:

"Dog breath" gets treated as an inevitable quirk, but persistent, noticeably bad breath is frequently an early, treatable warning sign, not just a normal trait.

When It's a Warning Sign

Persistent, strong odor — beyond typical mild dog breath — often indicates dental disease, including tartar buildup and gum inflammation.

Other Accompanying Signs

Visible tartar, red or swollen gums, and reluctance to chew hard food alongside bad breath strengthen the case for a dental issue.

What to Do

Persistent bad breath warrants a dental check rather than being dismissed as normal, since early dental disease is far easier to treat than advanced cases.

Frequently Asked Questions

**Is some level of dog breath always normal?**
Mild, non-offensive breath can be typical, but strong, persistent odor usually indicates a problem.

**Can diet affect breath odor?**

cat-dental-disease-signs-missed.content:

Subtle Signs

Reduced interest in hard food, dropping food while eating, subtle drooling, and reduced grooming can all indicate dental discomfort.

More Obvious Signs

Visible tartar, red or bleeding gums, and noticeable bad breath are clearer signs when present.

Why Regular Checks Matter

Given how well cats mask dental pain, routine dental checks during wellness visits catch disease that owners might otherwise miss entirely.

Frequently Asked Questions

**Do cats need their teeth brushed like dogs?**
Yes, it's beneficial though often harder to establish — ask your vet for practical tips.

**Is reduced grooming really linked to dental pain?**

**How often should cats have dental checks?**
Typically as part of regular wellness visits, at least annually.

dog-teeth-brushing-frequency.summary: The ideal brushing frequency for dogs, and practical tips for making it a sustainable habit.
dog-teeth-brushing-frequency.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

Daily brushing is the gold standard, but the realistic answer depends on what you and your dog can actually sustain long-term.

The Ideal Frequency

Daily brushing provides the most consistent dental benefit, closely mirroring how effective human dental hygiene works.

A Realistic Minimum

Even a few times a week provides meaningful benefit if daily brushing isn't sustainable for your household.

Building the Habit

Starting gradually, using dog-safe toothpaste, and building positive associations makes the habit more likely to stick long-term.

Frequently Asked Questions

**Can I use human toothpaste?**
No, use a pet-specific toothpaste — human toothpaste can contain ingredients unsafe for dogs.

**What if my dog won't tolerate brushing at all?**
Ask your vet about alternative dental support options, like specific dental chews or diets.

**Is it too late to start with an older dog?**
No, starting at any age still provides ongoing benefit, though existing dental disease may need addressing first.

why-dental-checkups-matter.title: Why Dental Checkups Matter for Dogs and Cats
why-dental-checkups-matter.summary: Regular dental checkups catch problems that home observation alone often misses. Here's why they're a standard part of preventive care.
why-dental-checkups-matter.content:

Home observation has real limits when it comes to dental health — much of what matters is only visible or assessable during a proper veterinary exam.

What a Dental Check Catches Early

Tartar buildup, early gum disease, and subtle changes that aren't visible or obvious from casual home observation.

Why Early Detection Matters

Early dental disease is significantly easier and less invasive to address than advanced disease, which can require more extensive treatment.

How Often

Typically part of routine wellness visits, with your vet advising more frequent checks if early findings warrant closer monitoring.

Frequently Asked Questions

**Can I assess dental health myself at home?**
You can spot obvious signs, but a full assessment, including under the gumline, needs a proper veterinary exam.

**Does every pet need a professional dental cleaning eventually?**
Many do, particularly as they age — your vet can advise based on individual dental health.

**Is anesthesia required for a proper dental cleaning?**

dog-obesity-how-to-know-overweight.title: Dog Obesity: How to Know If Your Pet Is Overweight
dog-obesity-how-to-know-overweight.summary: Obesity is one of the most common, and most preventable, health issues in dogs. Learn how to assess your dog's body condition.
dog-obesity-how-to-know-overweight.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

Obesity has become increasingly common in pet dogs, and it's genuinely linked to a range of downstream health problems — but it's also one of the most manageable when caught and addressed.

Assessing Body Condition

You should be able to feel (though not necessarily see) your dog's ribs with light pressure, and there should be a visible waist when viewed from above.

Why It Matters Beyond Appearance

Obesity is linked to joint stress, diabetes risk, and reduced lifespan — this isn't purely a cosmetic concern.

What to Do If Overweight

Work with your vet on an appropriate, gradual weight management plan rather than making significant diet changes without guidance.

Frequently Asked Questions

**Is it normal for certain breeds to carry more weight?**
Build varies by breed, but the rib and waist assessment remains a useful general guide across most breeds.

**Can obesity develop gradually without me noticing?**
Yes, which is why periodic body condition assessment, not just visual impression, matters.

**Should weight loss always be gradual?**
Yes, rapid weight loss can be unsafe — work with your vet on an appropriate pace.

healthy-diet-for-dogs-what-to-feed.title: Healthy Diet for Dogs: What Should You Feed Your Pet?
healthy-diet-for-dogs-what-to-feed.summary: A practical overview of what a balanced dog diet actually requires, beyond marketing claims on packaging.
healthy-diet-for-dogs-what-to-feed.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

Dog nutrition marketing can be overwhelming — here's a grounded overview of what a genuinely balanced diet actually requires.

Core Nutritional Needs

A balanced diet needs appropriate protein, fat, carbohydrates, vitamins, and minerals in proportions suited to your dog's life stage and size.

Commercial vs Home-Cooked

Both can be done well or poorly — as covered in our home-cooked food article, balance and proper formulation matter more than the format itself.

Individualizing the Plan

Age, breed size, activity level, and any health conditions should all factor into your dog's specific dietary needs.

Frequently Asked Questions

**Is grain-free always better?**
Not necessarily — this depends on your individual dog's needs, not a blanket rule.

**How do I know if my dog's current diet is balanced?**
Ask your vet to review it, particularly if home-cooking or considering a significant diet change.

**Should diet change with age?**
Yes, nutritional needs shift across puppy, adult, and senior life stages.

can-dogs-eat-eggs.title: Can Dogs Eat Eggs? Benefits, Risks, and Safe Feeding
can-dogs-eat-eggs.summary: Eggs can be a healthy addition to a dog's diet when prepared correctly. Here's what to know about benefits and risks.
can-dogs-eat-eggs.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

Eggs are a genuinely useful, protein-rich addition to many dogs' diets — as long as they're prepared and portioned correctly.

Benefits

Eggs provide high-quality protein and various nutrients that can be a healthy addition for many dogs in appropriate amounts.

Preparation Matters

Cooked eggs are generally recommended over raw, due to salmonella risk and biotin absorption concerns associated with raw egg whites.

Portion Control

Eggs should be an addition to, not a replacement for, a balanced diet — moderation matters.

Frequently Asked Questions

**Are raw eggs ever safe for dogs?**
Cooked is generally the safer recommendation due to bacterial risk and nutrient absorption concerns.

**Can eggs cause allergies in dogs?**
Yes, some dogs can be allergic or sensitive to eggs — introduce gradually and watch for reactions.

**How many eggs can a dog have?**
This depends on size and overall diet — ask your vet for guidance specific to your dog.

can-dogs-eat-rice-milk-curd.title: Can Dogs Eat Rice, Milk, or Curd?
can-dogs-eat-rice-milk-curd.summary: A practical breakdown of whether rice, milk, and curd are safe additions to a dog's diet.
can-dogs-eat-rice-milk-curd.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

These common Indian household staples come up often in dog diet questions — here's the practical answer for each.

Rice

Plain, cooked rice is generally safe and often used as a bland diet component for dogs with mild digestive upset.

Milk

Many adult dogs are lactose intolerant to varying degrees — milk can cause digestive upset and isn't necessary in a balanced diet.

Curd (Yogurt)

Plain curd in moderation is often better tolerated than milk due to lower lactose content, but introduce gradually and watch for reaction.

Frequently Asked Questions

**Is rice good for dogs with an upset stomach?**
Plain, cooked rice is commonly used as part of a bland diet during mild digestive upset — check with your vet for the full approach.

**Why is milk different from curd for dogs?**
Curd generally has lower lactose content, making it easier for some dogs to tolerate than plain milk.

**Should I introduce these foods gradually?**
Yes, introduce any new food gradually and watch for digestive reaction.

can-cats-eat-human-food.title: Can Cats Eat Human Food? Foods That Are Safe and Unsafe
can-cats-eat-human-food.summary: Some human foods are fine for cats in small amounts; others are genuinely dangerous. Here's a practical breakdown.
can-cats-eat-human-food.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

Cats are obligate carnivores with specific nutritional needs, which makes the human-food question more nuanced than for dogs.

Generally Safe in Small Amounts

Plain cooked chicken or fish (boneless), small amounts of plain cooked egg, and small bits of certain vegetables can be reasonable occasional additions.

Genuinely Dangerous

Onions, garlic, chocolate, caffeine, alcohol, grapes and raisins, and xylitol (found in some sugar-free products) are all toxic to cats.

Why Moderation and Caution Matter

Even safe foods shouldn't replace a nutritionally complete cat food — cats have specific dietary needs, like taurine, that general table food doesn't reliably provide.

Frequently Asked Questions

**Is tuna safe for cats regularly?**
Occasional small amounts are generally fine, but regular tuna feeding isn't recommended due to mercury content and nutritional imbalance.

**Can cats have dairy?**
Many cats are lactose intolerant — dairy isn't necessary and can cause digestive upset.

**What's the biggest risk food for cats specifically?**
Onions and garlic are particularly toxic to cats even in small amounts.

Commercial Food

Formulated commercial diets are designed to meet complete nutritional standards, offering convenience and consistency.

Homemade Food

Can offer more control over ingredients but requires careful formulation to avoid nutritional gaps — improperly balanced homemade diets are a real, common risk.

Whichever path you choose, proper formulation matters more than the format itself — consult your vet, especially for homemade diets, to ensure nutritional completeness.

Not automatically — it depends entirely on proper formulation and balance.

**Can I mix homemade and commercial food?**

sudden-diet-changes-digestive-problems.title: Why Sudden Diet Changes Can Cause Digestive Problems in Pets
sudden-diet-changes-digestive-problems.summary: Switching your pet's food too quickly is a common, avoidable cause of digestive upset. Here's why gradual transitions matter.
sudden-diet-changes-digestive-problems.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

A sudden food switch is one of the most common, entirely preventable causes of digestive upset in pets — the fix is simple but often skipped.

Why Gut Bacteria Need Time to Adjust

Your pet's digestive system adapts to their current diet over time; an abrupt change doesn't give gut bacteria time to adjust accordingly.

The Gradual Transition Approach

Mixing increasing proportions of new food with decreasing old food over about a week is a standard, effective transition approach.

When to Still Watch Closely

Even gradual transitions can occasionally cause mild upset in sensitive pets — monitor stool and appetite during any diet change.

Frequently Asked Questions

**How long should a diet transition take?**
Roughly 7-10 days is a common general guideline, though sensitive pets may benefit from a longer transition.

**Is this necessary for treats too?**
Less critical for occasional treats, but a new regular food component should still be transitioned gradually.

**What if my pet refuses the new food during transition?**
Adjust the ratio more slowly, or consult your vet if the refusal persists.

how-much-feed-puppy-kitten.title: How Much Should You Feed Your Puppy or Kitten?
how-much-feed-puppy-kitten.summary: Feeding amounts for growing puppies and kittens depend on several factors. Here's how to figure out the right amount.
how-much-feed-puppy-kitten.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

Overfeeding and underfeeding are both real risks during the rapid growth period — getting portions right matters more than in adulthood.

Why This Differs from Adult Feeding

Growing puppies and kittens have higher caloric and nutritional needs relative to body size than adult pets, requiring more frequent, carefully portioned meals.

Using Food Packaging Guidelines Correctly

Package guidelines are a starting point based on current weight and expected growth, not a fixed rule — adjust based on actual body condition.

Working with Your Vet

Regular weigh-ins during growth help fine-tune portions to your specific pet's actual growth trajectory, not just generic guidelines.

Frequently Asked Questions

**Should I free-feed a growing puppy or kitten?**
Scheduled meals are generally recommended over free-feeding to monitor intake and prevent overfeeding.

**How often should growing pets be weighed?**
Regularly during rapid growth phases — ask your vet for a specific schedule.

**Can overfeeding during growth cause long-term issues?**
Yes, particularly in large-breed puppies, where growth rate management matters for joint development.

senior-dog-health-checkup-tests.summary: Senior dogs benefit from more comprehensive monitoring than younger adults. Here's what a senior checkup typically covers.
senior-dog-health-checkup-tests.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

Senior dogs face a different risk profile than younger adults, which is why their checkups are typically more comprehensive, not just more frequent.

Why Senior Checkups Differ

Age-related conditions — kidney disease, arthritis, heart disease, cognitive changes — become more likely, warranting closer monitoring.

Common Components

Bloodwork, blood pressure assessment, joint and mobility evaluation, and dental checks are common additions to a senior wellness visit.

Frequency

Many vets recommend senior checkups every six months rather than annually, given how quickly some conditions can progress.

Frequently Asked Questions

**What age counts as senior for dogs?**
This varies by breed size — larger breeds are often considered senior earlier than smaller breeds.

**Is bloodwork always included in senior checkups?**
Commonly recommended, though your vet will advise based on your dog's specific history.

**Can early detection meaningfully change outcomes?**
Yes, for several common senior conditions, earlier detection generally supports better management.

senior-cat-care-common-problems.summary: Senior cats are prone to specific conditions that benefit from early detection. Here's what to watch for.
senior-cat-care-common-problems.content:

Senior cats face a fairly predictable set of common conditions — knowing them helps you and your vet watch proactively rather than reactively.

Common Conditions

Kidney disease, hyperthyroidism, dental disease, and arthritis are among the most common conditions seen in senior cats.

Why Cats Mask These Well

Cats' tendency to hide illness means these conditions often progress further before becoming visibly obvious than they would in a more expressive species.

The Value of Regular Monitoring

Regular senior wellness checks, including bloodwork, catch these conditions earlier than waiting for obvious symptoms.

Frequently Asked Questions

**At what age is a cat considered senior?**
Generally around 7 years and older, though this can vary.

**Is weight loss always concerning in senior cats?**
It's a common early sign of several conditions and should be evaluated rather than dismissed as normal aging.

**How often should senior cats have checkups?**

arthritis-in-dogs-signs-treatment.title: Arthritis in Dogs: Early Signs and Treatment Options
arthritis-in-dogs-signs-treatment.summary: Arthritis is common in aging dogs but often mistaken for normal slowing down. Learn to recognize the real early signs.
arthritis-in-dogs-signs-treatment.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

"He's just getting older" is often the explanation owners give for symptoms that are actually treatable arthritis, not an inevitable part of aging.

Early Signs

Stiffness after resting, reluctance to jump or climb stairs, slower to rise, and reduced activity level can all indicate early arthritis.

Why Early Recognition Matters

Earlier intervention can improve comfort and slow progression compared to addressing arthritis only once it's significantly advanced.

Treatment Options

Management often includes a combination of weight control, appropriate exercise, joint support, and pain management tailored to the individual dog.

Frequently Asked Questions

**Is arthritis only a senior dog condition?**
It's more common in seniors but can affect younger dogs too, particularly with joint conditions like hip dysplasia.

**Can weight management really help arthritis?**
Yes, significantly — reduced joint load is one of the most effective supportive measures.

**Is arthritis reversible?**
Not typically reversible, but well managed with appropriate treatment to maintain comfort and mobility.

kidney-disease-cats-warning-signs.summary: Kidney disease is one of the most common conditions in senior cats. Learn the early signs that often go unnoticed.
kidney-disease-cats-warning-signs.content:

Kidney disease is common enough in senior cats that recognizing the early signs — often subtle — can meaningfully change how the condition is managed.

Early Signs

Increased thirst and urination, mild weight loss, and reduced appetite are often among the earliest, subtlest indicators.

Why Early Detection Matters

Kidney disease is generally progressive, and earlier detection allows management strategies to potentially slow progression more effectively.

Diagnosis

Bloodwork and urine testing together provide the clearest picture of kidney function and disease stage.

**Can kidney disease be cured?**
Generally managed rather than cured, though management can significantly support quality of life.

Yes, specific dietary management is often a key part of the treatment approach.

Kidney disease affects dogs as well as cats, though the typical age and progression pattern can differ somewhat between species.

Symptoms

Increased thirst and urination, appetite loss, weight loss, and lethargy are common signs, though early stages may be subtle.

Treatment often involves dietary management alongside addressing any underlying or contributing causes, tailored to the individual dog's stage and situation.

diabetes-dogs-cats-symptoms-management.summary: Diabetes is increasingly diagnosed in pets. Learn the symptoms, how it's diagnosed, and what ongoing management looks like.
diabetes-dogs-cats-symptoms-management.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

Diabetes in pets is manageable with proper veterinary guidance — recognizing the symptoms early makes that management considerably easier.

Common Symptoms

Increased thirst and urination, increased appetite alongside weight loss, and lethargy are classic signs in both dogs and cats.

Diagnosis

Blood glucose testing, alongside other bloodwork and urine testing, confirms diagnosis and helps guide the management plan.

Ongoing Management

Treatment typically involves a combination of diet management and, often, insulin therapy, with regular monitoring to adjust the plan as needed.

Frequently Asked Questions

**Is diabetes more common in certain breeds or body types?**
Obesity is a recognized risk factor in both dogs and cats, alongside other individual risk factors.

**Can diabetes be reversed?**
In some cats, diabetes can go into remission with early, appropriate management — this is less typical in dogs.

**Does diabetes management require lifelong commitment?**
Generally yes, ongoing monitoring and management are typically needed long-term.

liver-disease-dogs-signs-diagnostics.title: Liver Disease in Dogs: Signs and Veterinary Diagnostics
liver-disease-dogs-signs-diagnostics.summary: Liver disease can progress silently before visible symptoms appear. Learn the signs and how it's typically diagnosed.
liver-disease-dogs-signs-diagnostics.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

The liver has significant functional reserve, which means liver disease can be quite advanced before obvious symptoms appear — making diagnostic screening valuable.

Possible Signs

Reduced appetite, lethargy, vomiting, changes in thirst, and in more advanced cases, yellowing of the gums or eyes (jaundice).

Why Symptoms Can Be Subtle Early On

The liver's functional reserve means significant damage can occur before clinical signs become obvious to an owner.

Diagnosis

Blood biochemistry testing is typically the first step, sometimes followed by imaging or further specific testing based on findings.

Frequently Asked Questions

**Can liver disease be caused by diet?**
Certain dietary factors can contribute, alongside other causes like toxins, infections, and age-related changes.

**Is jaundice always present with liver disease?**
No, it's a sign of more advanced disease, not present in all or early cases.

**Can liver disease be managed long-term?**
Depending on the cause and severity, many cases can be managed with appropriate veterinary care and diet.

heart-disease-dogs-symptoms.summary: Heart disease in dogs can develop gradually. Learn the symptoms that warrant veterinary evaluation.
heart-disease-dogs-symptoms.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

Heart disease in dogs often develops gradually, which means early symptoms can be easy to attribute to normal aging or reduced fitness.

Symptoms to Watch For

Coughing, reduced exercise tolerance, rapid breathing at rest, and fainting or collapse episodes can all indicate heart disease.

Why Early Detection Matters

Earlier management can help slow progression and maintain quality of life longer compared to addressing advanced disease.

Diagnosis and Monitoring

A physical exam (including listening to the heart), alongside imaging and sometimes specialized cardiac testing, helps diagnose and stage heart disease.

Frequently Asked Questions

**Are certain breeds more prone to heart disease?**
Yes, some breeds have higher genetic predisposition to specific cardiac conditions.

**Can heart disease be managed with medication?**
Yes, many cases are managed effectively with appropriate medication and monitoring.

**Is coughing always heart-related?**
No, but persistent coughing, especially in older dogs, warrants evaluation to rule out cardiac causes.

heartworm-disease-dogs-prevention.title: Heartworm Disease in Dogs: Prevention and Early Detection
heartworm-disease-dogs-prevention.summary: Heartworm disease is transmitted by mosquitoes and can be serious if untreated. Learn about prevention and detection.
heartworm-disease-dogs-prevention.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

Heartworm disease, transmitted through mosquito bites, is a genuinely serious condition where prevention is significantly easier than treatment.

How It Spreads

Heartworm larvae are transmitted through mosquito bites, meaning any dog with mosquito exposure carries some risk.

Why Prevention Is Preferred

Prevention through regular medication is considerably simpler, safer, and less costly than treating an established heartworm infection.

Detection

Regular testing, as recommended by your vet, can catch infection before it becomes advanced, particularly important given the delayed symptom onset typical of this disease.

Frequently Asked Questions

**Is heartworm a concern in India?**
Regional risk varies — ask your vet about local prevalence and appropriate prevention.

**Can heartworm affect indoor dogs?**
Yes, if mosquitoes have any access to the indoor environment.

**How often should dogs be tested?**
Your vet can advise a testing schedule appropriate to local risk and your dog's prevention status.

can-dogs-cats-get-dengue.summary: Dengue is a mosquito-borne human disease — here's what pet owners should actually know about dengue and their pets.
can-dogs-cats-get-dengue.content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Pritesh Vidhate, BVSc & AH, MVSc (Veterinary Epidemiology & Preventive Medicine).

With dengue a genuine seasonal concern for households, pet owners reasonably wonder whether their dog or cat is at similar risk.

The Short Answer

Dengue virus, as understood in human medicine, is not considered a significant natural disease concern in dogs and cats the way it is in humans.

Why Mosquito Control Still Matters for Pets

While dengue itself isn't the primary pet concern, mosquitoes do transmit other diseases relevant to pets, like heartworm, making control still worthwhile.

What to Actually Watch For

If your pet shows fever, lethargy, or other illness during a household dengue concern, treat it as its own medical situation and consult your vet rather than assuming dengue.

Frequently Asked Questions

**Should I worry about my dog if my family has dengue?**
Focus on standard mosquito control for the household; dengue isn't considered a primary natural risk for dogs specifically.

**Are pets a source of dengue transmission?**
No, dengue transmission is mosquito-to-human, not through pet contact.

**Should mosquito control still be a priority for pet owners?**
Yes, for other pet-relevant mosquito-borne risks like heartworm.

Standing water and contaminated puddles can carry infection risk — discourage drinking from puddles during walks.

Shorter, well-timed walks avoiding heavy rain and standing water are a reasonable adjustment.

**Does wet fur really increase infection risk?**
Yes, trapped moisture creates conditions favorable for skin and ear infections — dry thoroughly after outdoor time.

**Are exotic pets affected by monsoon differently?**

Provide adequate warmth, particularly for short-haired breeds, seniors, and very young pets, and monitor for signs of discomfort in cold conditions.

Birds

Birds are sensitive to temperature drops and drafts — maintaining a stable, appropriately warm environment matters more in winter.

Rabbits

Outdoor or semi-outdoor rabbits need protection from cold drafts and adequate bedding; monitor for reduced activity that could signal discomfort or illness.

This varies by species and individual — short-haired, senior, and young pets generally benefit most from extra precautions.

can-pets-get-human-flu-colds.summary: Pets can catch respiratory illness, but it's usually not the same virus as human flu or colds. Here's the actual relationship.
can-pets-get-human-flu-colds.content:

It's a reasonable question when someone in the house is sick — but the relationship between human respiratory illness and pet illness is more nuanced than direct transmission.

The General Answer

Most common human cold and flu viruses are not typically transmitted to dogs and cats — these species have their own distinct respiratory pathogens.

Pet-Specific Respiratory Illness

Dogs and cats have their own respiratory conditions (like kennel cough or cat flu) that aren't the same as human cold or flu viruses.

When to Still Be Cautious

If your pet shows respiratory symptoms while a household member is sick, it's more likely coincidental illness or a pet-specific pathogen — evaluate it on its own merits with your vet.

Frequently Asked Questions

**Should I isolate my pet if I have the flu?**
Not typically necessary for standard human flu, but general hygiene practices are still reasonable.

**Can my pet catch COVID-19 from me?**

**Are pet respiratory illnesses contagious to other pets?**

dogs-cats-transmit-diseases-humans.summary: Some pet diseases can transmit to humans (zoonotic diseases). Learn which ones matter and how to reduce risk practically.
dogs-cats-transmit-diseases-humans.content:

Zoonotic disease — illness transmissible between animals and humans — is a real but manageable consideration for pet-owning households.

Common Zoonotic Concerns

Rabies, certain parasites, ringworm, and some bacterial infections are among the recognized zoonotic risks relevant to dog and cat ownership.

Practical Risk Reduction

Regular veterinary care, deworming, vaccination (particularly rabies), and good hygiene practices meaningfully reduce zoonotic risk.

Higher-Risk Groups

Young children, elderly individuals, and immunocompromised people warrant somewhat extra caution around zoonotic risk, though this doesn't mean avoiding pets.

Frequently Asked Questions

**Does this mean I should be afraid of my pet?**
No, routine preventive care makes zoonotic risk genuinely manageable for typical households.

**Is handwashing after pet contact really important?**
Yes, it's a simple, effective risk-reduction habit worth maintaining consistently.

**Are all pet diseases zoonotic?**
No, many common pet conditions have no human transmission risk at all.

Consistent veterinary preventive care, good hygiene, and prompt attention to any pet illness together form the core of practical risk reduction.

A scheduled deworming routine, not just reactive treatment when symptoms appear, keeps parasite levels consistently low.

Prompt waste cleanup, handwashing after pet contact, and regular veterinary deworming together form an effective combined approach.
